So the hooks are a seatbelt. What stops a write is the credentials: a run should hold none that can apply, mutate a cluster, or write to a cloud account.

docs.title: Recommended setup for runs that touch infrastructure
docs.text:
1. Read-only credentials by default. Gatework's live evidence (plan, diff, describe) needs reads only (targets in state.json). Give runs credentials that can do nothing else:
  2. AWS: a dedicated profile that assumes a role with ReadOnlyAccess (or a narrower ViewOnlyAccess plus the specific reads you need). Export only that AWS_PROFILE; keep admin profiles out of the run's shell and ~/.aws/config if you can.
  3. Kubernetes: a kube context whose user is bound to the built-in view ClusterRole, in a separate kubeconfig (KUBECONFIG=~/.kube/ai-readonly). view can't read Secrets.
  4. Terraform/Terragrunt: plan with the read-only role and -lock=false, against a backend the role can read but not write. Applies happen in CI (Atlantis, Spacelift, a pipeline) after merge, with credentials the agent never sees.
  5. GitHub: a fine-grained token limited to the repos in play, without admin or workflow-write scope. Deliver needs only contents and pull-request write.
  6. Sandbox the run. Run the harness in a devcontainer, VM, or the harness's own sandbox (Claude Code's sandboxed Bash, Codex workspace-write sandbox mode), with only the read-only credentials mounted and network egress limited to what the run needs.
  7. Keep write paths out of reach. Production kube contexts, state buckets, and break-glass roles should not exist on the machine the agent runs on. If they must, use a separate OS user or profile for agent sessions.
  8. Hooks still on. They catch the honest mistakes early and prompt before outward actions, which keeps the Deliver gate meaningful.

With this setup, a bypassed hook produces an access-denied error rather than a change.

docs.title: Gaps by tool
docs.text:
OpenCode runs the same guards through a plugin (overrides/opencode/plugin.js), with one difference: a plugin can't prompt, so anything the guards would ask about is blocked, and the model is told to ask you to run it yourself. A pack's guard rules apply under its [scope], judged from the bash tool's workdir, else the session's directory, and a pack's deny reads as a refusal. MCP tools get the outward guard too: OpenCode names them <server>_<tool>, so the plugin asks OpenCode which servers are connected and matches the longest, and the guard reads the call as mcp__<server>__<tool>. Run in a real OpenCode (1.19.6). A pack can ship its own OpenCode plugin as overrides/opencode/plugin.js; apply links it beside core's, and the lock records it with the pack's hooks (packs).

Cursor runs them through overrides/cursor/hooks/guard.py on beforeShellExecution (both guards) and beforeReadFile (secrets), from ~/.cursor/hooks.json (brainrc) or the plugin's .cursor-plugin/hooks.json. Cursor's ask was reported broken and reads accept only allow or deny, so ask becomes deny there too. A pack's guard rules apply under its [scope], judged from the event's cwd (else the first workspace root), and a pack's deny reads as a refusal, not as a call to ask you. File writes and MCP calls aren't guarded in Cursor: it has no reliable pre-write hook. Not yet run in a real Cursor: it is tested with payloads shaped like the hook input in the cursor-hooks types.

Codex runs them through overrides/codex/hooks/guard.py on PreToolUse, from $CODEX_HOME/hooks.json: shell commands get both guards, MCP tools the outward guard, and apply_patch the secrets guard (each file it adds or changes, with its added lines). Codex's PreToolUse takes only allow and deny, and treats an ask as a failed hook that lets the call run, so ask becomes deny there too. A pack's guard rules apply under its [scope], judged from the payload's cwd; Codex names an MCP server's tools with its - turned into _, and a rule matches either spelling. Codex runs a hook only after you trust it: open /hooks in Codex once after brainrc apply. Until then it skips the hooks without a word, codex exec included. Hosted tools such as web search don't reach the hook. Run in a real Codex (0.172), shell, apply_patch, code mode and MCP calls alike.

Antigravity runs them through overrides/antigravity/hooks/guard.py on PreToolUse for run_command, from ~/.gemini/config/hooks.json, where brainrc's hooks sit under their own entry, brainrc. A guard's ask replies force_ask, which prompts even for a command you allowed before, and a deny replies deny. With no objection it replies allow, which Antigravity's docs define as handing the call on to the next hook or the default policy, so your own permission settings still decide; it is not auto_approve. In headless agy -p, which can't prompt, an ask ends as a deny. A pack's guard rules apply under its [scope], judged from the command's Cwd, else the first workspace path. File tools and MCP tools aren't guarded there yet: the docs don't name their arguments or how MCP tools are called. Not yet run in a real Antigravity: it is tested with payloads shaped like the docs' run_command example.

Five more tools run them through their own overrides/<tool>/hooks/guard.py, each turning its tool's call into Claude Code's (#307 to #312). None has been run in the live tool yet: each is tested with payloads shaped like its docs, and where the docs don't name a tool's arguments the guard reads the likely fields and lets anything else through.

  • GitHub Copilot (~/.copilot/hooks/brainrc.json, preToolUse): shell (bash, powershell) gets both guards, view reads and create or edit writes the secrets guard. It replies permissionDecision: deny; Copilot acts on no ask, so ask becomes deny. MCP calls aren't guarded: the docs don't say how Copilot names them. Copilot denies a call whose preToolUse hook fails, so the hook is written as bash, never run by PowerShell, and it lets the call through when it can't run (no python3) or can't read the call.
  • Devin Local (~/.config/devin/config.json, PreToolUse): exec, read, write, edit and mcp__<server>__<tool>. It replies decision: block, so ask becomes a block. Its payload has no working directory, so a pack's [scope] is judged from $DEVIN_PROJECT_DIR.
  • Kiro (~/.kiro/hooks/brainrc.json, PreToolUse on every tool): execute_bash, fs_read, fs_write, str_replace and mcp_<server>_<tool>. A command hook blocks by exiting non-zero with the reason on stderr, so ask becomes a block, and the guard exits 0 for anything it can't read, and when there's no python3: a failure would block the call. Kiro CLI loads ~/.kiro/hooks as global hooks.
  • JetBrains Junie (~/.junie/config.json, PreToolUse): Claude Code's tool names, so its calls reach the guards as they are, and it replies decision: ask or deny, so an ask stays an ask. Junie runs hooks from your user config only, not a project's.
  • Gemini CLI (~/.gemini/settings.json, BeforeTool, off by default): run_shell_command, read_file, write_file, replace and mcp_<server>_<tool>. It replies decision: deny, so ask becomes deny.

Kiro and Gemini CLI name an MCP tool mcp_<server>_<tool>, and a server's name may hold _ too, so their guards split the name by the servers in the tool's own MCP config (user and project), the longest that fits.

Amp has no command hooks: its only hook point is a TypeScript plugin API, which brainrc doesn't write yet, so Amp gets your instructions and MCP servers but no guard.

docs.title: Harness packages
docs.text: What each harness supports for installing brainrc as a native package, without a clone. Research for #50, done 2026-10-08. Formats change fast: re-check a harness's docs before building its package. Gemini CLI was retired for consumer accounts on 2026-06-18; Antigravity CLI replaced it.

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text: Harness Package and install Rules without a clone Hooks Agents Packs Claude Code .claude-plugin/ (shipped); /plugin install SessionStart hook output (10,000-char cap) yes: allow, ask, deny yes, as <plugin>:<name> (gatework:brainrc-work) plugin dependencies with semver ranges Codex .codex-plugin/ or .claude-plugin/ (verified); codex plugin marketplace add owner/repo no plugin route: ~/.codex/AGENTS.md or config developer_instructions yes: PreToolUse, SessionStart TOML roles in config; not shippable in a plugin separate plugin; no dependencies found Antigravity CLI root plugin.json (shipped, unverified); agy plugin install <git url> plugin rules/*.md with trigger: frontmatter yes: PreToolUse ask or deny; no known "no opinion" reply markdown, agents/ separate plugin; no dependencies found OpenCode JS plugin (npm or ~/.config/opencode/plugins/): hooks and tools only instructions[] config or AGENTS.md blocks by throwing; no ask markdown files with a different frontmatter plugin[], instructions[], skills.paths Cursor .cursor-plugin/plugin.json (shipped, unverified); symlink a checkout to ~/.cursor/plugins/local/ plugin rules/ with alwaysApply: true yes: allow, deny; ask reported broken markdown, agents/ separate plugin; a .cursor-plugin/marketplace.json lists several

docs.title: Claude Code
docs.text:
Sources: hooks, plugin components, dependencies, plugin CLI.

  • Rules: a plugin SessionStart hook's stdout, or hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext, is added to context. Matchers startup|resume|clear|compact re-inject after /clear and compaction. Over 10,000 characters, Claude sees a 2,000-character preview only. A plugin-root CLAUDE.md, rules, and most settings are not loaded. claude plugin validate accepts the hook (checked here); that the text reaches the model is unconfirmed (needs a live session).
  • Packs: "dependencies": [{"name": "brainrc", "version": "^0.3"}] installs core with a pack; versions resolve to git tags <plugin>--v<version>. claude plugin list --json lists installed plugins with their paths. A pack skill dispatching a core agent across plugins is unconfirmed.
  • Hooks from several plugins all run; deny > ask > allow.

docs.title: Codex
docs.text:
Source: openai/codex at 529cd6b (the docs site was blocked here): codex-rs/core-plugins/, codex-rs/hooks/, codex-rs/agent-roles/.

  • Reads .claude-plugin/marketplace.json and .claude-plugin/plugin.json as well as its own .codex-plugin/. Verified with Codex 0.161.0: codex plugin marketplace add <repo> and codex plugin add brainrc@brainrc install our plugin unchanged. Gatework's plugin (brainrc/gatework) works the same way. The install copy drops symlinks (skills/brainrc-gatework/roles), so Gatework falls back to ../../agents/.
  • Skills come from the manifest's skills field when it has one, and only from there, so Gatework's names ./skills/ as one string, the form Codex's docs give. Core's own plugin has no skills.
  • Skills: native, ~/.agents/skills (~/.codex/skills deprecated). Custom prompts are deprecated for skills; a plugin's commands/ become skills, except any that use $ARGUMENTS (verified: all five of ours were skipped). Core now ships them as user-invoked skills, which Codex installs.
  • Hooks: PreToolUse, SessionStart, and more, from a plugin's hooks/hooks.json. Whether a SessionStart hook can inject rules is unconfirmed.
  • Agents: [agents.<role>] TOML; a plugin can't ship them.

docs.title: Antigravity CLI
docs.text:
Google's docs site was blocked here and agy (closed source) couldn't be installed, so this comes from public sources: the antigravity-cli CHANGELOG and issues (#403, #1053, #1059), and plugins that record tested behavior (MemPalace, CoalHearth v2.8.0 on agy 1.3.1). Nothing here was run against a real agy.

  • A plugin is a folder with plugin.json (its schema requires name and rejects unknown keys; a skills path or list adds skill folders to skills/, and nothing names other folders), plus optional skills/, agents/, rules/, hooks.json, and mcp_config.json. agy plugin install <git url> needs plugin.json at the repo root. No commands/: skills are the slash commands. Install may copy only the folders it recognises (#403).
  • Rules: rules/*.md load only with frontmatter naming a trigger (always_on, model_decision, glob, manual); files without one are dropped silently.
  • Hooks: hooks.json at the plugin root, {"<name>": {"PreToolUse": [{"matcher", "hooks"}]}}; commands run from the plugin folder. PreToolUse gets toolCall: {name, args} (run_command → args.CommandLine; view_file, write_to_file, replace_file_content) and prints {"decision": "ask" | "deny", "reason"}. An empty {} is reported to deny every call. Its hooks page (read 2026-11-26) now lists allow (hand on to the next hook or the default policy), auto_approve, deny, ask, force_ask and deny_unless_prior_grant, and #1053 shows allow doesn't approve a command the user hasn't granted, so allow is the "no objection" reply core's guard uses through brainrc apply (~/.gemini/config/hooks.json). The plugin route is still unshipped.
  • Skills: disable-slash-command hides a skill from /; disable-model-invocation is likely ignored.

docs.title: OpenCode
docs.text:
Source: sst/opencode docs source at a697115 (the docs site was blocked here): packages/web/src/content/docs/.

  • A plugin is a JS module: hooks (tool.execute.before), tools, and system-prompt transforms. It can't ship agent, skill, or command files, so the package is a config dir plus a small plugin.
  • Agents need a transform (#19, shipped in 0.3.19): Claude's tools: Read, Grep makes OpenCode's whole config invalid (verified, 1.18.35); it wants permission, model as provider/model-id, and mode: subagent.
  • Guard plugin: tool.execute.before can block by throwing and permission.ask can answer a prompt OpenCode already shows, but a plugin can't force a prompt, so "ask" becomes "deny".
  • Skills: native, ~/.config/opencode/skills/ (also reads ~/.claude/skills/).

docs.title: Cursor
docs.text:
cursor.com is blocked from where this was built, so the format comes from Cursor's official plugin repo, cursor/plugins (checked 2026-10-09 at ccb5507: schemas/, its plugins, and its create-plugin scaffold skill), plus hook payload types from the community cursor-hooks package.

  • Manifest: .cursor-plugin/plugin.json, only name required, unknown keys rejected. skills, agents, rules, commands take relative paths; hooks a path or an inline object. Our generated manifest validates against schemas/plugin.schema.json.
  • Local install: a plugin directory, or a symlink to one, at ~/.cursor/plugins/local/<name>/. A search result says Cursor falls back to .claude-plugin/ when .cursor-plugin/ is missing, so we ship our own: Cursor rejects Claude's hook format.
  • Rules: description, alwaysApply, optional globs frontmatter; Cursor's examples use .mdc. Whether a plugin loads .md rules is unconfirmed.
  • Agents: name, description, model, readonly. Whether Cursor accepts our model: sonnet values is unconfirmed.
  • Hooks: {"version": 1, "hooks": {"<event>": [{"command": ...}]}}, user file ~/.cursor/hooks.json, ${CURSOR_PLUGIN_ROOT} in plugin hooks. beforeShellExecution gets {command}, beforeReadFile {file_path, content}; the reply is {permission, user_message, agent_message}. permission: ask was reported broken in 2.4.21 and reads take only allow or deny.

docs.title: What this means
docs.text:
1. One generated .claude-plugin/ serves Claude Code and Codex; Cursor gets .cursor-plugin/. Antigravity needs a root plugin.json; OpenCode needs a config dir plus a JS hook plugin.
  2. Commands should become skills, or be generated per harness: Codex skips $ARGUMENTS commands and Antigravity has no commands.
  3. Rules and pack extensions need rendering outside the checkout ($BRAINRC_HOME), then each harness loads them its own way. Codex plugins have no rules route yet.
  4. Guard hooks need a deny fallback: only Claude Code reliably supports ask.

docs.title: Proposed order for #50
docs.text:
1. Render to $BRAINRC_HOME; Gatework reads extensions from there (every harness needs it).
  2. Codex through the existing .claude-plugin/: test the install, convert commands to skills.
  3. Antigravity plugin: root plugin.json, rule triggers (done, unverified); hooks after a live test.
  4. OpenCode: agent transform (#19, done); guard plugin (deny only) done in 0.3.25.
  5. Cursor: .cursor-plugin/ plugin and guard hooks (deny only) done in 0.3.26; unverified in a real Cursor.
  6. Installable brainrc (uv tool install or pipx install, from GitHub and later PyPI, core bundled): done in 0.3.22. Packs by git URL, fetched by brainrc (git + ref, brainrc update): done in 0.3.23.

docs.title: Hook latency and a native guard
docs.text: The roadmap allows native hooks only on evidence (#299). This is the evidence, measured against the owner's bar: if a tool call's p95 hook latency is over about 50 ms, port the guard evaluator to Go; if it's under, stay in Python. A full rewrite is off the table either way.

docs.title: How it was measured
docs.text:
scripts/hook_latency.py runs the hooks each tool call fires the way the tool runs them: the command from overrides/claude/settings.fragment.json through sh -c, a fresh python3 per hook, and the matching hooks of one Claude Code call in parallel. The hook-latency workflow ran it with 100 runs per case (after 3 warm-ups) on GitHub's runners, Python 3.12, three times on 2026-11-16. Session start includes E28's MCP pin check, with one pinned local stdio server.

Median / p95 in ms. Linux is ubuntu-latest (x86_64), the steadiest of its three runs; macOS is macos-latest (arm64), one column per run, because the runs disagree.

Call Hooks Linux macOS run 1 macOS run 2 macOS run 3 Baseline: sh + python3 -c pass 0 7.9 / 8.1 27.6 / 52.4 24.8 / 50.5 39.9 / 78.9 Claude Code, Bash 2 19.1 / 20.9 30.7 / 34.9 41.3 / 67.1 83.3 / 112.0 Claude Code, Bash pipeline 2 19.6 / 20.8 31.4 / 40.8 37.0 / 64.4 75.5 / 107.7 Claude Code, Read 1 18.6 / 19.3 28.5 / 29.9 37.5 / 61.2 67.7 / 110.8 Claude Code, Edit 1 19.2 / 19.9 28.6 / 32.0 41.3 / 66.4 70.8 / 96.2 Claude Code, MCP tool 1 15.7 / 16.5 26.0 / 28.1 41.1 / 69.5 48.9 / 87.8 Cursor, shell command 2 56.7 / 58.8 79.4 / 96.8 108.3 / 167.4 172.8 / 225.6 Cursor, file read 1 38.8 / 43.5 56.0 / 69.3 77.0 / 124.7 142.8 / 210.5 Session start, no pins (once) 1 26.2 / 28.0 35.5 / 36.8 48.7 / 77.0 78.4 / 105.1 Session start, 1 pinned server (once) 1 38.7 / 50.7 69.0 / 79.8 74.6 / 97.7 107.8 / 139.8

Across Linux's three runs, a Claude Code call's p95 stayed between 16 and 27 ms. Rerun with python3 scripts/hook_latency.py, or the workflow on a pull request that touches the hooks.

docs.title: Against the 50 ms bar
docs.text:
• Linux: under. A Claude Code call's p95 is at most 27 ms in every run. About 8 ms of it is starting Python; the guard work is the rest.
  • macOS: over in two of three runs. A Claude Code call's p95 was 28 to 41 ms in the first run, 61 to 70 ms in the second and 88 to 112 ms in the third.
  • Cursor: over everywhere, because its guard.py starts a second Python for each guard.
  • On macOS, most of the time is starting the interpreter, not the guard logic: an empty python3 -c pass alone had a p95 of 50 to 79 ms on those runners. The runners are shared VMs, so a developer's own Mac is likely faster, but these numbers are the evidence on hand.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text:
By the bar, macOS is over, so port the guard evaluator to Go, and nothing else. For the port to help, the hook a tool runs has to be the Go binary itself: a Python hook that calls a Go evaluator still pays for starting Python, which is most of the time measured here. The cheap Cursor fix (its guards in one process) is worth doing either way.

No Go work has started; it waits for the owner's go-ahead.

docs.title: Install
docs.text: brainrc is a Python command. The quickest way to get it is uv, which also fetches a Python 3.11+ if your machine has none. You need git too: brainrc uses it to fetch packs.

docs.title: Install with uv
docs.text:
uvx brainrc status          # try it first: lists what apply would write, writes nothing
uv tool install brainrc
brainrc apply
brainrc status              # prints "Everything in sync."

That's it. apply writes into each AI tool installed on this machine and skips the others. Run brainrc init before apply if you want to choose which tools brainrc manages, or how much it installs; getting started walks through it.

If your shell can't find brainrc after the install, run uv tool update-shell and open a new shell.

docs.title: Other ways to install
docs.text:
How Command Notes pipx pipx install brainrc Same as uv. If brainrc isn't found, run pipx ensurepath. Homebrew brew install brainrc/tap/brainrc From the brainrc/homebrew-tap tap. npx npx github:brainrc/brainrc status Runs brainrc through uvx, so it needs uv but no Python. Good for a one-off run, not for apply. Keep the github:: brainrc isn't on npm. Claude Code plugin /plugin install brainrc@brainrc Claude Code only, no rules or packs. See plugins. A clone git clone https://github.com/brainrc/brainrc For changing brainrc itself. See below.

Run apply from an installed command, not from uvx or npx: apply links your tools into the installed package, and those two run brainrc from a cache that can be cleared.

docs.title: Pin a version
docs.text: Install a given release with uv tool install brainrc==<X.Y.Z> (or pipx install brainrc==<X.Y.Z>, uvx brainrc@<X.Y.Z>, npx github:brainrc/brainrc#v<X.Y.Z>). Releases are listed on PyPI and in the CHANGELOG.

docs.title: Update
docs.text:
uv tool upgrade brainrc     # or: pipx upgrade brainrc, brew upgrade brainrc
brainrc apply --repair

--repair relinks anything that still points at the old version. Moving packs to newer commits is a separate step, brainrc update (upgrading).

Coming from the old names, ai-config or spec-agent? Upgrading has the steps.

docs.title: Uninstall
docs.text:
brainrc uninstall --dry-run     # see what goes
brainrc uninstall               # remove everything apply put into your tools
uv tool uninstall brainrc       # or: pipx uninstall brainrc, brew uninstall brainrc

uninstall keeps your own settings, hooks and MCP servers, and puts back any instructions file init moved aside. uninstall --purge also deletes brainrc's own folder (~/.config/brainrc): your local config and the packs it fetched (troubleshooting).

docs.title: From a clone
docs.text:
Clone brainrc when you want to change brainrc itself. Run the same commands through scripts/brainrc.py:

git clone https://github.com/brainrc/brainrc ~/brainrc
cd ~/brainrc
python3 scripts/brainrc.py init      # optional: pick tools and a profile
python3 scripts/brainrc.py status
python3 scripts/brainrc.py apply

Two things differ from an installed command:

  • Your local files live in the checkout (harnesses.local.toml, packs.local.toml, brainrc.local.toml, rules/*.local.md), not in ~/.config/brainrc/. Git ignores them.
  • Links point into the checkout, so git pull updates every tool at once. Re-run apply after a pull that changes rules, since rules are rendered, not linked. To stay on a release, check out its tag (git checkout v<X.Y.Z>) and re-run apply.

If you move the checkout, run python3 scripts/brainrc.py apply --repair from the new place. CONTRIBUTING.md covers the checks to run before a pull request.

docs.title: Platforms
docs.text: macOS and Linux. brainrc installs by symlink. On a Windows machine that can't make one (no Developer Mode, not an administrator), apply copies instead and records each copy (link_mode), so skills, agents, commands and rules install without WSL. On Windows apply also writes each of brainrc's hooks as one Python call (py -3 -I -c "...", falling back to python) instead of a POSIX shell line, in the field each tool's docs give for it: Claude Code's exec form, Codex's commandWindows, Copilot's powershell, and command for the rest. macOS and Linux get exactly the lines they got before. A Windows CI cell that runs without symlinks is on the roadmap.

docs.title: MCP servers
docs.text: A pack can define MCP servers once, in mcp/servers.toml, and apply writes them into each tool's own config. brainrc core ships none; they come from your packs. Only the full profile installs them, and full is the default (configuration).

docs.title: Add a server
docs.text:
In your pack's mcp/servers.toml:

[servers.acme-github]
command = "npx"
args = ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-github"]
env_from = ["GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN"]   # names only; the value stays in your environment
harnesses = ["claude", "codex"]               # optional; default: every tool brainrc writes MCP servers for

[servers.acme-docs]
url = "https://docs.example.com/mcp"          # an HTTP server instead of a command

A server's name starts with the pack's prefix, like its other items. Then run brainrc apply. Close Claude Code first: it rewrites ~/.claude.json while it runs, and apply refuses to write a file that changed under it.

docs.title: Where they go
docs.text:
Tool File Written as Claude Code ~/.claude.json mcpServers Codex ~/.codex/config.toml a marked [mcp_servers] block OpenCode ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json mcp (opencode.jsonc when only that exists, keeping its comments) GitHub Copilot ~/.copilot/mcp-config.json mcpServers, each with tools: ["*"] Devin Local ~/.config/devin/mcp_config.json mcpServers; variables as ${env:NAME} Kiro ~/.kiro/settings/mcp.json mcpServers; Kiro expands ${NAME} only for variables in its approved list Amp ~/.config/amp/settings.json amp.mcpServers (settings.jsonc when only that exists) JetBrains Junie ~/.junie/mcp/mcp.json mcpServers, with no env: Junie reads no variable references, so the server gets them from the environment Junie runs in Gemini CLI ~/.gemini/settings.json mcpServers; a remote server as httpUrl

Antigravity and Cursor aren't supported yet.

docs.title: Secrets stay out of files
docs.text: env_from names environment variables; brainrc writes a reference the tool expands when it starts the server (${NAME}, env_vars, {env:NAME} or ${env:NAME}), never the value; Junie, which reads no reference, gets none. validate rejects a server with an env table, which would hold values.

docs.title: Your own servers are safe
docs.text: brainrc only replaces or removes servers it wrote itself (it keeps a list in ~/.config/brainrc/mcp-owned.json). If you already defined a server of the same name, apply reports a CONFLICT and leaves yours alone. A backup of the file is written before every change.

docs.title: Pin their tools
docs.text:
An MCP server can change what its tools do after you approved it. brainrc pin-mcp guards against that for Claude Code:

brainrc pin-mcp

It starts each stdio server brainrc installs, lists its tools, shows what changed since the last pin, and on your yes records a hash of each tool's definition. At the start of each Claude Code session a hook checks the tools again. If one changed, it warns you and tells the model not to call it until you run pin-mcp again. HTTP servers aren't pinned, and the check gets 4 seconds for all servers together: a server it can't reach in that time is skipped (guardrails).

apply names each stdio server whose tools aren't pinned yet.

The full format is in formats.

docs.title: Packs reference
docs.text:
A pack is a folder or git repo of rules, skills, agents, commands, hooks and MCP servers, with a pack.toml that names it. brainrc layers each pack you turn on over its own rules and guard hooks, and installs the lot into every tool. This page is the reference: every file, key and rule.

  • Learn: your first pack builds one, step by step.
  • Do: use a pack, import the files you have, validate a pack in its own CI, or start a pack for an employer, a team, yourself or a stack, or from a Claude Code plugin.
  • Understand: why packs, and what you trust when you enable one.
  • Copy: examples/pack-acme (every feature but hooks) and examples/pack-homelab (a guard hook).

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
Every folder is optional.

acme-ai-pack/
  pack.toml              name, prefix, extensions for other packs (see Extensions)
  validator.py           optional checks and renders of its own (see Validator plugins)
  tests/                 the pack's own tests, which validate --pack runs (see Pack tests)
  skills/acme-*/         linked into each tool's skills folder
  agents/acme-*.md       linked into each tool's agents folder
  commands/acme-*.md     linked into each tool's commands folder
  rules/NN-*.md          rendered after all core rules, as one labelled block (see Rules)
  overrides/claude/hooks/                 linked to <hooks_dir>-acme (e.g. ~/.claude/hooks/brainrc-acme)
  overrides/claude/settings.fragment.json merged after the core fragment; {{hooks_dir}} = the pack's hooks dir (see Permissions)
  overrides/opencode/plugin.js            linked beside core's guard plugin, as brainrc-guard-acme.js
  mcp/servers.toml       MCP servers, synced after core's (see formats.md#mcp-servers-mcpserverstoml)
  tripwires.toml         patterns that must not appear in the pack (checked by validate)

Skills, agents, commands, and MCP servers must start with the pack's prefix, and no name may exist in two sources unless exclude leaves one copy out; apply refuses to write anything while one does. The full rules are in Naming, and each file's format in formats.

docs.title: Packs from one repo
docs.text:
A repo can hold several packs, one per folder, each with its own pack.toml. subdir next to git and ref names the folder that is the pack:

[python]
git = "https://github.com/brainrc/packs.git"
ref = "v0.1.0"
subdir = "python"   # a folder inside the repo, using /; no `.` or `..`

apply fetches the repo into $BRAINRC_HOME/packs/<key> and installs from that folder; the rest of the repo is never read. It fails, naming the folder, if the ref has no such folder or it's a link rather than a folder; the clone stays at the commit it had. The lock records subdir next to git, ref and commit, so install --frozen and check install and compare that folder at the locked commit (lock format). Each pack keeps a clone of its own, so two packs from one repo can sit at different refs. subdir works the same in a repo's brainrc.toml.

docs.title: pack.toml
docs.text:
name = "acme"
prefix = "acme-"          # default: "<name>-"
id = "acme/acme-ai-pack"  # optional: the <owner>/<pack> ID it's published under (see Naming)
requires_core = ">=0.7, <0.9"   # core versions this pack works with (see Compatibility)
max_always_tokens = 800   # optional budget for rules + descriptions (see Context cost)
test = "tests"            # optional: tests validate --pack runs (see Pack tests)

[scope]                   # optional: where the pack applies (see Scope)
remotes = ["github.com/acme/*"]

[[guard.deny]]            # optional: commands core's guard refuses here (see Guard rules)
match = "acme-deploy prod"
reason = "deploys to production"

[extensions.gatework]      # what Gatework reads; see Extensions
deliver_checks = [        # listed in the Deliver gate as done / not applicable / not run
  "Deploy plan reviewed by the owning team",
]

[[extensions.gatework.domains]]   # extra rows for Gatework's Domains table
files = "`deploy/*.yaml`, `charts/acme-*`"
skills = ["acme-deploy"]
reviewer = "brainrc-infra-reviewer"

[[extensions.gatework.intake_context]]   # skills Gatework runs after fetching the ticket
skill = "acme-context"
when = "every ticket"

[extensions.gatework.ticket]   # a connector for this pack's ticket refs, with its config
connector = "brainrc-ticket-jira"
refs = ["ACME-*"]
host = "acme.example.net"
blocked_status = "Blocked"
instructions = "Link the PR in the ticket's Development panel."   # see Connector config

validate checks pack.toml against schemas/pack.toml.schema.json: a known key with a value of the wrong type fails, and a key it doesn't know warns, naming the closest known key (max_always_token → max_always_tokens), since brainrc would otherwise ignore it. Only validate reports these; apply still installs the pack.

docs.title: Keys
docs.text:
Generated from pack.toml.schema.json by scripts/pack_reference.py:

Key Type What it is name string The pack's name; default: its packs.toml table or folder name. prefix string What every skill, agent, command and MCP server name starts with; default: "<name>-" (naming). id string The <owner>/<pack> ID the pack is published under (naming). description string One line on what the pack is for. requires_core string Core versions the pack works with, e.g. ">=0.8, <0.9" (compatibility). max_always_tokens number Budget for the tokens the pack loads into every session: rules plus descriptions (context cost). validator string A Python module in the pack that checks what only it understands (validator plugins). test string The pack's own unittest tests, a directory or a .py file in the pack; validate --pack runs them (pack tests). scope table Where the pack applies: any glob matching means it does; none means everywhere (scope). guard table [[guard.deny]] and [[guard.ask]] rules core's guard hook enforces, with match or tool, reason and scope; deny rules may name a path or host for the OS sandbox instead (guard rules). extensions table Tables other packs read, one per namespace, e.g. [extensions.gatework]; the pack that owns a namespace checks it (extensions).

docs.title: Editor completion
docs.text:
A pack's pack.toml and mcp/servers.toml have JSON Schemas in docs/schemas/ (pack.toml, mcp-servers.toml), as does core's harnesses.toml. Editors that use Taplo (VS Code's Even Better TOML, Zed, Helix) complete keys and flag wrong ones from a first line naming the schema, which brainrc import writes for you:

#:schema https://raw.githubusercontent.com/brainrc/brainrc/main/docs/schemas/pack.toml.schema.json
name = "acme"

In a checkout of this repo, .taplo.toml maps each file to its schema. Files outside it (a pack's own repo, ~/.config/brainrc/harnesses.local.toml) take the #:schema line.

docs.title: mcp/servers.toml
docs.text:
Each [servers.<name>] table is one MCP server, named with the pack's prefix (MCP servers). A server has command or url, not both; an HTTP server takes no args or env_from. Generated from mcp-servers.toml.schema.json:

Key Type What it is command string A stdio server: the program to run. args array of strings Arguments for command. url string An HTTP server: its URL. env_from array of strings Environment variables the harness passes to command; names only, never values. harnesses array of strings The harnesses that get this server; default: every one brainrc writes MCP servers for.

docs.title: What new pack writes
docs.text:
brainrc new pack <name> writes a pack that validates on its first run, with everything its own repository needs (options):

brainrc new pack acme              # writes ./acme, then checks it as validate --pack does
brainrc validate --pack acme
File What it's for pack.toml name, prefix, requires_core for this core's minor series, a token budget and test rules/10-<name>.md one short rule: load the facts skill instead of guessing skills/<prefix>facts/SKILL.md the facts agents would otherwise guess: repositories, hosts, tools, teams tripwires.toml a tripwire against home folder paths; add one for each stale fact tests/test_pack.py pack tests: rules stay short, no secret values README.md, AGENTS.md how to use the pack, and the rules for whoever edits it; CLAUDE.md and GEMINI.md point at AGENTS.md for the tools that need it .github/workflows/validate.yml, .pre-commit-config.yaml the validate-pack action and hook, pinned to this core's tag .gitignore keeps *.local.* files and caches out

In a terminal it asks for the name, prefix, the tools you'll edit the pack with, and a ticket system (github, jira or local), which becomes an [extensions.gatework.ticket] table. It checks the naming rules before it writes anything, never writes into a folder with files in it but .git (--force replaces an earlier pack and keeps its .git), and --enable adds the pack to packs.local.toml.

examples/pack-template holds the same files for a pack called mypack, with steps for renaming it: the contents of a GitHub template repository, for anyone who would rather start from Use this template than install brainrc first. scripts/pack_template.py keeps it in step with new pack, and CI validates it.

docs.title: What new <item> writes
docs.text:
Inside a pack, brainrc new <kind> <name> writes one item that validates, with the prefix applied and its frontmatter filled in, then checks the pack as validate --pack does (options). It finds the pack from the folder you are in, or takes --pack DIR, and never replaces an item without --force.

Command Writes new skill <name> skills/<prefix><name>/SKILL.md with name and description new skill <name> --domain GLOB,... a domain skill: Validate (offline), Conventions, Review checklist and Never without approval, and a Domains row for those files in pack.toml new agent <name> agents/<prefix><name>.md with read-only tools (Read, Grep, Glob), model = inherit, and the handoff block it ends with new rule <name> rules/NN-<name>.md after the last rule, with trigger: always_on and alwaysApply: true; it prints the pack's always-loaded tokens against max_always_tokens new command <name> commands/<prefix><name>.md with description and $ARGUMENTS; --as-skill writes the user-invoked skill form Codex runs (formats)

The bodies come from brainrc/_templates/items: headings with one line each that says what goes there. Replace them before you publish the pack.

docs.title: Naming
docs.text:
A clear name is the cheapest trust signal a pack has. Every pack follows these seven rules:

  1. brainrc- and brainrc/ are reserved for official packs. No other pack's name, prefix or ID starts with them.
  2. A registry prefix starts with the owner's handle. A pack published as jdoe/k8s-tools uses a prefix such as jdoe- or jdoe-k8s-.
  3. No vendor names without verification. A pack's name, prefix and ID don't use a vendor's name (aws, github, openai and the like) unless the vendor itself is verified as its owner.
  4. No names one or two edits from an official name. The official names are brainrc and the IDs in the table below, so brainrx- and brianrc/review are refused.
  5. ASCII lowercase letters, digits and hyphens only, in names, prefixes, IDs and item names.
  6. A prefix is 2 to 24 characters, not counting its trailing hyphen.
  7. Item names are prefix-scoped. Every skill, agent, command and MCP server starts with the pack's prefix, so two packs' items can't collide.

validate and apply refuse a pack that breaks one. The vendor names and the official IDs it checks are listed in brainrc/naming.py.

A pack's ID is <owner>/<pack>, where the owner is the GitHub user or organization that publishes it. Official packs are owned by brainrc. Gatework has a repo of its own; the others are folders of brainrc/packs, enabled with subdir (packs from one repo):

ID What it holds Issue brainrc/gatework the default pack: Gatework's engine, its roles, ticket connectors and general domain skills (brainrc/gatework) #172 brainrc/starter the small, measured base for the default profile (starter) #313 brainrc/review review, PR description, commit message and unslop (review) #314 brainrc/go Go, built from today's brainrc-go-service skill (go) #315 brainrc/terraform-aws Terraform and AWS (terraform-aws) #316 brainrc/kubernetes Kubernetes, including GitOps and containers (kubernetes) #317 brainrc/python Python: Ruff and pytest (python) #183 brainrc/node-ts Node and TypeScript: tsc and ESLint (node-ts) #184 brainrc/rust Rust: rustfmt, Clippy and cargo test (rust) #185 brainrc/security-baseline the default guard policy, secret protection and a sandbox profile (security-baseline) #323

brainrc/go, brainrc/terraform-aws and brainrc/kubernetes hold the domain skills Gatework shipped up to 0.8, under the same names (#318). Gatework 0.9 no longer ships them, so enable the packs for the stacks you use to keep those skills. If you pin Gatework 0.8, enable one beside it by excluding Gatework's copy in brainrc.local.toml, for example exclude = ["gatework:skills/brainrc-kubernetes"]: an excluded item isn't installed, so it doesn't collide. brainrc/starter and brainrc/review reuse Gatework's names too (brainrc-project-commands, and the review, PR description, commit message and unslop skills): they are for a setup with Gatework off.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
The rendered instructions file has three parts, in this order:

  1. Core rules, in filename order.
  2. Each enabled pack's rules, one block per pack in packs.toml order, filename order inside. Each block starts with <!-- pack: <name> --> and a line telling the model the rules refine the ones above.
  3. *.local.md rules from any source, under <!-- local -->.

Pack rule numbers only order rules within the pack. Later rules refine earlier ones and must not contradict them: a pack rule that contradicts core is a bug in the pack. Write it as a narrower case ("in Acme repos, also ...") instead.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
[scope] says where a pack applies, so a work pack's deliver checks, guard rules and reviewers stay out of your personal repos, in place of free text such as "in acme repos":

[scope]
remotes = ["github.com/acme/*", "git.acme.example.net/*"]   # a git remote of the repo you're in
paths = ["~/src/acme"]          # the directory you're in, or one above it; ~ and $VARS expand
kube_contexts = ["acme-*"]      # kubectl's current context ($KUBECONFIG or ~/.kube/config)
aws_profiles = ["acme-*"]       # $AWS_PROFILE, "default" when it isn't set
tickets = ["ACME-*"]            # a ticket ref in the branch name (acme-42-fix), or one passed in

Every value is a list of globs, and the pack applies when any one of them matches. A remote is matched as written and as host/owner/repo, so one glob covers its SSH and HTTPS URLs. A pack without [scope], or with an empty one, applies everywhere, as before. The rules, skills and agents a pack installs are still installed everywhere: scope decides where its extensions and guard rules take effect.

brainrc scope lists each enabled pack as APPLIES or SKIPPED in the directory you're in and says why, and brainrc scope --extensions prints the extensions a run there should read: only the packs that apply. The extensions.md that apply renders holds every pack and ends with a Scope section saying where each scoped pack applies.

docs.title: Guard rules
docs.text:
A pack adds rules to core's guard in pack.toml, without a hook of its own:

[[guard.deny]]                 # refused
match = "acme-deploy prod"
reason = "deploys to production, which only the release pipeline does"

[[guard.ask]]                  # asked about first
tool = "mcp__acme-jira__*transition*"
reason = "moves an Acme ticket to another status"
scope = { kube_contexts = ["acme-*"] }   # optional: in place of the pack's [scope]

Each rule sets reason and one of match or tool. match is a command: its program (by name, from any directory, after VAR=value, sudo or env) and then the other words in that order, with other words and flags allowed between them; each word may be a glob. tool is a glob for an MCP tool's full name. A rule takes effect only where the pack's [scope] matches the directory the command runs in, or the rule's own scope when it sets one.

apply renders every enabled pack's rules, with their scopes, into $BRAINRC_HOME/guard-rules.json, and core's guard_outward.py checks them on every Bash and MCP call. Commands inside sh -c, eval, $(…) and backticks are unwrapped as for core's own rules. A pack's deny wins over any ask; a pack's ask is shown when core has nothing to ask. Without the file (no rules, or before the first apply), the guard behaves as before. validate checks each rule. Claude Code, Cursor, OpenCode, Codex and Antigravity all enforce them through core's guard, judging the scope where each runs the command; where a tool can't ask, a pack's ask blocks the call and tells the model to ask you to run it (guardrails).

A [[guard.deny]] rule can set path or host instead, to reach what the hooks can't see (a script that reads a file, a client that calls a host). apply compiles these into Claude Code's sandbox settings in ~/.claude/settings.json, which the OS enforces on every Bash command and its child processes:

[[guard.deny]]
path = "~/.acme/credentials"   # sandbox.filesystem.denyRead and denyWrite
reason = "Acme's deploy keys"
scope = {}                     # the sandbox applies everywhere, so say so in a scoped pack

[[guard.deny]]
host = "*.acme.example"        # sandbox.network.deniedDomains
reason = "Acme's internal services"
scope = {}

path starts with ~/ or /; host is a domain, optionally *. first. These rules can't ask and can't follow a [scope], so validate refuses one under [[guard.ask]] or one that a scoped pack leaves scoped. The entries brainrc adds are recorded in settings-owned.json, as permission entries are: your own stay, and the pack's go when it's disabled or brainrc is uninstalled. They take effect only where Claude Code's sandbox is on (sandbox.enabled), and the sandbox covers Bash, not the Read tool or web fetches (guardrails). Other tools have no sandbox brainrc can write, so there these rules do nothing.

Test a rule with brainrc.testing against core's hook, with BRAINRC_HOME set to a directory holding the rendered file, and a near miss beside the risky command.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
A pack's overrides/claude/settings.fragment.json can list permission entries, so it ships a read-only allow list or hard denies without a hook:

{
  "permissions": {
    "allow": ["Bash(acme-status:*)", "mcp__acme-jira__get_issue"],
    "deny": ["Bash(acme-deploy prod:*)"]
  }
}

apply adds each allow, deny and ask entry to the settings file after yours, and records the ones it added in $BRAINRC_HOME/settings-owned.json. Disable the pack and the next apply removes exactly those: an entry you had before the pack, or one another enabled pack still lists, stays. uninstall takes them out too. Other keys under permissions (defaultMode, say) are set only when the file has none, and stay. brainrc.lock records every entry as one of the pack's tool grants, so apply lists a new one as PERMS and asks first (why packs). The minimal profile installs no settings fragment, so a pack's permissions and hooks need recommended or full.

docs.title: Extensions
docs.text:
[extensions.<namespace>] is a table another pack reads; core passes it through untouched. The pack that owns the namespace checks it with its validator plugin, and validate warns about a table no enabled pack reads. Gatework, the default pack, owns [extensions.gatework] above. apply renders every enabled pack's table into $BRAINRC_HOME/extensions.md (default ~/.config/brainrc/extensions.md), which Gatework reads at intake. With no other packs enabled, the file says so and Gatework runs as before; with Gatework disabled, there is no file.

The file also lists, under Pack roles, every agent the other packs install, with the path of its file. A pack's agent adds to Gatework's roles and never replaces one, and a harness that installs no agents (Codex, Antigravity, Cursor) can still run it as a role in the one-session fallback by reading that file. The acme example's acme-reviewer is one.

A machine can add its own [extensions.gatework] in brainrc.local.toml (configuration); extensions.md lists it after every pack's.

The old forms from before 0.7.0, the same keys directly under [extensions] or under [extensions.spec-agent], still work with a warning: move them under [extensions.gatework].

A pack has at most one [extensions.gatework.ticket]: one connector and the refs it handles. A team with two ticket systems splits them into two packs. The connector, core or the pack's own, must follow the connector contract, which validate checks.

docs.title: Connector config
docs.text:
A connector skill declares the keys its table takes, and their types, in its SKILL.md frontmatter under the Agent Skills metadata map, so every harness still loads it:

---
name: acme-ticket-desk
description: Ticket connector for the Acme service desk. Use for DESK- refs.
metadata:
  brainrc-config: "refs: list required; queue: integer; blocked_status: string"
---

Each key: type entry is one of string, integer, boolean or list (of strings), followed by required when the table must set it. validate then checks every pack table that names the skill as its connector: a key of the wrong type or a missing required key fails, and a key the connector doesn't declare warns. Only validate reports these; apply still installs the pack. A connector that declares nothing, or a declaration with a mistake (which fails on the skill), isn't checked. Every table may also set instructions: what the pack tells the connector about its tickets, in place of free-form keys such as notes. It reaches the model, so the pack's tripwires check it like the pack's other text, unless a tripwire sets paths or excludes pack.toml.

docs.title: Validator plugins
docs.text:
A pack can check what only it understands: validator = "validator.py" in pack.toml names a Python module in the pack. Each name in it is optional:

Name What core does with it NAMESPACE the [extensions.<namespace>] table it owns (default: the pack's name) LEGACY_KEYS, LEGACY_NAMESPACES, REMOVED_IN older extension forms it still reads; validate warns until REMOVED_IN check_extensions(table, where, skill_names, agent_names) errors in one pack's table, before apply writes anything warn_extensions(table, where) warnings for one pack's table, from validate check(me, sources) errors across every source, from validate doctor(me) (FAIL or WARN, what, fix) findings for doctor render_extensions(tables) the text of $BRAINRC_HOME/extensions.md

A validator is the pack's code running inside brainrc, so core runs it only for a default pack (core's packs.toml pins it, or your own packs.local.toml points it elsewhere), for the pack validate --pack checks, and for a pack whose entry in packs.local.toml sets run_validator = true. Otherwise validate warns that the pack ships one. Gatework's validator.py is the reference.

docs.title: Pack tests
docs.text:
test = "tests" in pack.toml names the pack's own unittest tests: a directory (its test*.py files) or one .py file. validate --pack runs them in a fresh Python, from the pack's root, and fails if one fails or none is found. They are the pack's code, so only validate --pack from the command line runs them; doctor and apply never do.

brainrc.testing runs a guard hook the way Claude Code does, a PreToolUse payload on stdin, so a test needs no scaffolding of its own. A string is a Bash command; a dict is the whole payload:

from brainrc.testing import assert_allows, assert_asks, assert_denies, assert_no_opinion, run_hook

HOOK = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "overrides/claude/hooks/guard_acme.py"

class GuardTest(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_asks_before_a_deploy(self):
        assert_asks(HOOK, "acme deploy prod")      # the risky command
        assert_allows(HOOK, "acme deploy --help")  # and a safe near-miss

assert_allows passes when the hook allows or has no opinion, and assert_no_opinion only when it stays out, so Claude Code's own permission check still decides; assert_denies counts exit code 2 as a deny. Each lists every case that came out wrong, and a missing, failing or hung hook fails. run_hook(hook, payload) returns the decision itself. pack-homelab has a full example.

docs.title: tripwires.toml
docs.text:
Stale facts that must not come back, checked by validate:

[[tripwire]]
id = "old-pager"
pattern = '(?i)\bpagerbot\b'
message = "pagerbot was replaced by the new on-call tool"
allow = '(?i)replaced|decommissioned|never'   # lines matching this pass (they warn against it)
paths = ["*.md"]                              # default; fnmatch against the path in the pack

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text:
brainrc's version is in VERSION. CHANGELOG.md tags changes that affect packs with [pack contract]. Declare the versions your pack supports with requires_core: comma-separated clauses of >=, >, <=, <, ==, != and a version (missing parts are zero, and a bare version means >=).

  • Not satisfied → validate fails and apply/status write nothing, naming the pack.
  • Missing → allowed, with a warning.
  • Policy: semver. While core is 0.x, a breaking pack-contract change bumps MINOR, so pin ">=0.N, <0.N+1". After 1.0, breaking changes bump MAJOR: pin ">=1.N, <2". Other changes (new skills, fixes, docs) bump PATCH and never break a pin.

docs.title: Context cost
docs.text:
brainrc tokens estimates tokens per skill, agent, and command across all enabled sources. It also shows what loads in every session (rules and descriptions) versus on use. Keep pack rules short: they load in every session on that machine.

validate enforces a budget on each source's always-loaded tokens (its rules plus its skill, agent, and command descriptions). Core's is 3,000. A pack declares its own in pack.toml:

max_always_tokens = 800

Over a declared budget, validate fails and names the biggest items. A pack without max_always_tokens gets a warning above 1,000 tokens. Any description over 100 tokens gets a warning: say what the skill does and when to use it, and move the rest into the body.

docs.title: What validate checks
docs.text: This checks the core, the default packs on disk and that pack, whatever else is in packs.toml: frontmatter; pack.toml against its schema; cross-references in skills, agents, commands, rules, README.md and docs/** (relative links, [agent: x] tags, and skills named as "x skill" or in prose as "the x skill"; pack files may reference core's and Gatework's skills and agents); the naming rules; collisions; extension references and connector config; requires_core; tripwires; and the pack's own tests. A skill named in prose counts only when its name has a hyphen and starts with the pack's prefix or a first part two known skills share, so "the follow-up skill" stays prose. A relative link in a rule warns, since rules are rendered into each harness's own file; link a URL. apply refuses a pack only for what would break the install (frontmatter, names, collisions, tags, links in skills, agents and commands); the rest only validate reports.

docs.title: Plugins
docs.text:
Most tools can also install brainrc as a plugin, with no brainrc command. There are two plugins:

  • brainrc (this repo): the guard hooks, and the rules where a tool's plugins can load them.
  • gatework (brainrc/gatework): Gatework's skills (/brainrc-work and the rest) and its agents.

Install both to get close to what brainrc apply installs.

docs.title: Plugins or the brainrc command?
docs.text:
Plugins brainrc command Skills and agents yes, from gatework yes Guard hooks Claude Code and Cursor Claude Code, OpenCode and Cursor Rules Antigravity and Cursor only every tool Your own packs no yes Lockfile, check, audit no yes

Use one, not both, for each tool: together they load every skill and hook twice. doctor warns when it sees both in Claude Code or Cursor (fix).

docs.title: Claude Code
docs.text:
/plugin marketplace add brainrc/brainrc
/plugin install brainrc@brainrc
/plugin marketplace add brainrc/gatework
/plugin install gatework@gatework

Plugin skills are named after their plugin, so Gatework's command is /gatework:brainrc-work. Claude Code plugins can't load rules into every session: for the rules, copy rules/*.md from this repo into your own ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md.

docs.title: Codex
docs.text:
codex plugin marketplace add brainrc/brainrc
codex plugin add brainrc@brainrc
codex plugin marketplace add brainrc/gatework
codex plugin add gatework@gatework

Codex gets Gatework's skills (call them by name, such as brainrc-work) and the agent files Gatework reads. Codex plugins can't carry rules: copy rules/*.md into ~/.codex/AGENTS.md, or use the brainrc command. Whether Codex runs the brainrc plugin's guard hooks is not yet verified (research).

docs.title: Antigravity CLI
docs.text:
agy plugin install https://github.com/brainrc/brainrc
agy plugin install https://github.com/brainrc/gatework

The first brings the rules, the second the skills. Antigravity has no place for agents in a plugin, so Gatework reads its role files directly. Guard hooks aren't included yet: use agy's own permission settings. This install was built from Antigravity's public docs and hasn't been run end to end (research).

docs.title: Cursor
docs.text:
Cursor loads a local clone as a plugin:

git clone https://github.com/brainrc/brainrc ~/src/brainrc
git clone https://github.com/brainrc/gatework ~/src/gatework
ln -s ~/src/brainrc ~/.cursor/plugins/local/brainrc
ln -s ~/src/gatework ~/.cursor/plugins/local/gatework

The first brings the rules and the guard hooks for shell commands and file reads (they deny instead of asking); the second brings the skills and agents. Cursor keeps its user rules in its Settings, not in a file, so this plugin is the only way brainrc's rules reach Cursor. Built from Cursor's official plugin repo and not yet run in a real Cursor (research).

docs.title: OpenCode
docs.text: OpenCode plugins are JavaScript modules that can't ship skills or agents, so there is no OpenCode plugin. Use the brainrc command.

docs.title: Post-deliver: following a PR to merge (design)
docs.text: Status: all five build steps are built (see references/watch.md). A run used to end at the Deliver gate: push, PR, ticket update, retro, stage: done, and whatever came next was fixed by hand. This page designs the stage that closes that loop. Build order is at the end.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• React to CI failures and review comments on the run's PR, inside the same gates and evidence rules as the rest of the run.
  • After merge, re-check the acceptance criteria on the default branch.
  • Record what happened after delivery in state.json and retro.md, so the metrics count rework done after the PR went up, not just before.

Non-goals: merging (always a human), deploying (still after merge, outside the run), and babysitting PRs the run didn't open.

docs.title: Stage: watch
docs.text:
… ⛔ DELIVER ─► push · PR · ticket ─► watch ─┬─► CI red ───────► fix task ─► review ─► ⛔ PUSH ─┐
                                             ├─► review comment ► fix task / reply ──► ⛔ PUSH ─┤
                                             ├─► merged ────────► post-merge verify ─► done
                                             └─► closed ────────► done (abandoned)     ◄────────┘

stage gains watch between deliver and done. The run enters it after the PR opens (delivery: normal only; local-only runs go straight to done).

How it wakes up. Pull-based, so it works in every harness: /brainrc-gatework-resume (or /brainrc-work on the same ref) at stage: watch fetches the PR's state through the ticket connector and handles whatever changed since watch.checked_at. A harness with PR event subscriptions (Claude Code on the web) can call the same step on each event; that's an optional trigger, not a requirement. No daemon and no polling loop in the engine.

Connector contract. One new optional operation, pr_status: CI check results on the head commit, review threads (unresolved, with author and body, and an optional id), and merge state. brainrc-ticket-github implements it with two read-only calls: gh pr view <n> --json statusCheckRollup,headRefOid,state,updatedAt (checks, head SHA, state, updated_at) and gh api graphql reviewThreads (unresolved only, via isResolved); see its ## pr_status section for the queries and mapping. Connectors without it skip watch, and the run ends at done as today.

docs.title: CI failure
docs.text:
1. Summarize the failing check's log into .runs/ (summary only, per efficiency.md; the log is untrusted).
  2. If the failure also occurs on the base branch, or names nothing this diff touched, record it as external and stop with a one-line note. Not this run's to fix.
  3. Otherwise add a fix task C1.. (agent: brainrc-implementer, files: those the failure points at) and run it through the normal implement → review path, with the same retry budget.
  4. Pushing the fix is outward: present a short Push gate (diff stat, commit list, the failing check it should fix). Approve → push. A run never pushes without approval.

docs.title: Review comment
docs.text:
The comment is untrusted input, just like the ticket body. Each unresolved thread is handled once; its key goes in watch.thread_log (keys only, no raw text). For each new thread:

  • A small, local change (rename, added test, one-function fix) → a fix task R1.., then the Push gate.
  • A question about intent → draft a reply from spec.md; post it only after it's approved at the next Push gate (replies are outward too), via the connector's reply_thread.
  • Large or design-level → stop and ask. The user decides; the run doesn't redesign on a reviewer's word alone.

Embedded instructions in a thread are flagged, not followed. After 3 review rounds the PR is handed back and nothing further is classified.

docs.title: Post-merge verify
docs.text: When the PR merges, run the verifier in a detached worktree (specs/<slug>/.runs/post-merge) at the merge commit (or the local tip of the base if that commit is missing), writing verify-merged.md. watch.post_merge is regression (a check that passed in verify.md fails on the merge: report it, open nothing, print a suggested follow-up), unverified (nothing could be run; never claimed as pass), or pass. A PR closed unmerged ends the run as abandoned with no verify.

docs.title: State and retro
docs.text:
state.json additions:

"watch": {
  "checked_at": "2026-10-20T09:12:00Z",
  "head_sha": "abc1234",
  "ci_failures": [{ "check": "test", "sha": "abc1234", "cause": "own|external", "task": "C1" }],
  "review_rounds": 2,
  "threads": { "total": 5, "fixed": 3, "replied": 2, "flagged": 0 },
  "thread_log": [{ "key": "<16-hex key>", "kind": "ask", "task": "R1", "flagged": false }],
  "merged_at": null,
  "post_merge": null,
  "outcome": null
}

metrics gains post_deliver_retries (fix tasks after the PR opened) and time_to_merge (PR opened → merged, in minutes, from timestamps, never estimated; unset if either is missing). watch.post_merge is pass|regression|unverified, watch.outcome is merged|abandoned.

retro.md keeps its sections and adds After delivery: CI failures (own/external), review rounds and what reviewers caught that the run's own reviewers didn't, post-merge result. The retro is first written at deliver as today, and this section is appended once when watch ends (merged or abandoned). The "what reviewers caught" line is the useful one: each miss is a candidate edit to a reviewer role or checklist.

docs.title: Build order
docs.text:
1. Metrics rollup first (scripts/retro_report.py). Aggregate state.json and retro.md across runs and projects: gate rework, first-pass review rate, retries, interventions, time per stage. It needs no new state, gives a baseline today, and is the place the watch numbers will land. Without it, the new fields would be written and never read. Done.
  2. pr_status in the connector contract and brainrc-ticket-github; validate accepts it as optional. Done.
  3. watch stage for CI failures and the Push gate. Done.
  4. Review comments. Done.
  5. Post-merge verify and the retro's After delivery section; add them to the rollup. Done.

Each step is one PR and ships with an eval: a sandbox ticket with a fake pr_status fixture (red CI, then a review comment, then merged), graded with scripts/evals.py check.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• Should the Push gate be skippable for fix-only pushes on a run's own branch? Default no: start strict and loosen with retro data.
  • After how many rounds should watch give up and hand the PR back? Proposal: the existing retry budget per fix task, plus a stop after 3 review rounds.

docs.title: Team setup: brainrc.toml and brainrc.lock
docs.text: Give a repo's AI agents the same skills and rules on every machine and in CI. You commit two files: brainrc.toml says which packs the repo uses, and brainrc.lock records exactly what they were. apply writes the agent files into the repo itself (.agents/skills/, AGENTS.md, ...), so every tool that opens the repo finds them, whether or not brainrc is installed there.

docs.title: Set it up
docs.text:
cd my-repo
printf 'version = 1\n' > brainrc.toml     # Gatework only; add packs below
brainrc apply                              # writes .agents/skills/, .claude/skills/ and brainrc.lock
git add brainrc.toml brainrc.lock .agents .claude
git commit -m "Add brainrc"

A teammate, or CI, then runs:

brainrc install --frozen    # exactly what the lock records, or fail
brainrc check               # exit 1 if anything drifted from the lock

To change what the repo uses, edit brainrc.toml and run apply, which relocks. To take newer pack versions, run brainrc update. Commit the result either way.

The rest of this page is the full contract for both files. It is language-neutral: another implementation that reads and writes them as described here is compatible. The JSON Schemas schemas/brainrc.toml.schema.json and schemas/brainrc.lock.schema.json describe each file after it is parsed as TOML; brainrc checks both files against them on every read. Conformance fixtures are in tests/fixtures/lockfile/.

docs.title: Scopes
docs.text:
• User scope is your machine: brainrc's own content, the default pack and the packs in packs.local.toml, linked into each installed tool's home folder. Its lock is $BRAINRC_HOME/brainrc.lock (default ~/.config/brainrc/brainrc.lock).
  • Project scope is a repo with brainrc.toml at its root. Its agent files are written into the repo, and its lock is brainrc.lock next to brainrc.toml. brainrc finds the project from the current directory: that directory or a parent, up to the repo root (the first directory that holds .git).

Both scopes apply together. The user's own config still layers on top of a project's at run time, because harnesses read the user's home and the repo.

docs.title: What apply writes in a project
docs.text:
brainrc apply (and status, which writes nothing) runs the user scope first, then the project in the current directory, under its own Project <dir> (brainrc.toml) heading.

  • Skills are copied, not linked, to .agents/skills/<name>/, so the repo works on every machine and in CI. A link inside a skill (Gatework's roles/) is copied as the files it points to.
  • Rules from the project's packs go into a marked block in AGENTS.md: <!-- brainrc:begin: … --> to <!-- brainrc:end -->. Your own text above and below the block stays. With no rules, there is no block, and a file that held only the block is removed.
  • Standard files first. Codex, OpenCode, Cursor and Antigravity read .agents/skills/ and AGENTS.md themselves, so they get nothing else. A tool that can't read them names its own places in harnesses.toml (project_skills, project_instructions). Today that is Claude Code only: skills are copied to .claude/skills/ too, and CLAUDE.md gets a marked block holding @AGENTS.md, unless it already reads AGENTS.md (a link to it, or its own @AGENTS.md line). harnesses in brainrc.toml picks which tools get their own files; drop one and its files and block are removed.
Tool Skills Instructions Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, Antigravity .agents/skills/ AGENTS.md Claude Code .claude/skills/ (copy) CLAUDE.md block importing AGENTS.md
  • Only the project's packs: core's rules and guard hooks, MCP servers and anything machine-local (packs.local.toml, brainrc.local.toml, *.local.md) stay in the user scope, so they never change a project's files.
  • Git packs are fetched by apply, never by status, into $BRAINRC_HOME/project-packs/<key>-<id>, one clone per URL and ref.
  • Ownership: brainrc.lock lists every file brainrc wrote (outputs). A file there is updated or removed as its pack changes. A file brainrc didn't write, or one you changed after it was removed from the packs, is a CONFLICT and is left alone.

docs.title: Pinned commits and update
docs.text:
apply resolves each git pack's ref once and records the commit in the lock. After that the commit is pinned: apply, status and install keep the pack at the lock's commit, on this machine and on a teammate's, even when the tag is moved or the branch (or the remote's default branch, for a pack with no ref) moves on. A clone found at another commit is put back (FETCH <pack> <url> (<ref>, locked at <commit>)). Changing git or ref in the config is a deliberate move, so the next apply fetches the new ref and relocks.

brainrc update [<pack> ...] is the one command that moves a pin to what the ref resolves to now. It refetches the named packs (every git pack when none is named; in a project, the project's packs of that name too) and, before anything is relinked or relocked, prints for each pack:

MOVED     gatework  v0.7.1: 753b9960c5e0 -> 8c41d2f0a9b3  (user scope)
          commit    8c41d2f Tighten the review checklist
          added     skills/brainrc-new/SKILL.md
          changed   skills/brainrc-work/SKILL.md

The commits are the ones between the old pin and the new one (up to 50; an older pin that isn't in them is named, as a rewritten history or a longer gap), and the files are the pack's installed files whose hash changed. CURRENT says nothing moved. Then it runs apply, which relocks. A failed fetch applies nothing, and the next apply puts the pack back at its pin.

docs.title: Installing from the lock
docs.text: brainrc install --frozen installs exactly what brainrc.lock records, for CI and teammates. It fetches each git pack's locked commit, never its ref, so a moved tag changes nothing. Every check runs before anything is written: the packs in brainrc.toml (or packs.toml) and the lock must match by key, URL, ref and path, and every file must hash as the lock says, outputs included. On any mismatch it names each one, writes nothing and exits 1. It never rewrites the lock and never removes files. It won't overwrite a file brainrc didn't write either: one at a locked path whose hash is neither the lock's nor what brainrc last wrote there on this machine (kept in $BRAINRC_HOME/project-state/), or a hand-edited block in AGENTS.md. It names each one and writes nothing; --force overwrites them. Neither writes through an AGENTS.md that is a link. The scope is the project when there is a brainrc.toml here or above, else the user; --scope user|project picks one. brainrc install without --frozen is apply.

docs.title: Checking for drift in CI
docs.text:
brainrc check exits 1 when anything differs from brainrc.lock, naming each difference: a pack in brainrc.toml the lock doesn't have (or the reverse), a pack file this machine has that hashes differently, a file brainrc owns in the repo that was edited, removed or added to, and its block in AGENTS.md. It uses no network and writes nothing. A git pack not fetched on this machine is checked through the repo's files; a clone at another commit than the lock's is reported as MOVED and doesn't fail (apply puts it back).

- uses: actions/checkout@v4
- name: Agent files match brainrc.lock
  run: pipx run brainrc check

brainrc install --frozen after it also fetches each git pack at its locked commit and checks it.

docs.title: brainrc.toml
docs.text:
version = 1                                  # optional; 1 is the only version
exclude = ["gatework:skills/brainrc-aws"]    # optional; items to leave out (see below)
harnesses = ["claude", "codex"]              # optional; tools that get their own files

[packs.gatework]        # a default pack: on unless `enabled = false`
ref = "v0.7.1"          # pin it to another ref; its `git` URL is kept

[packs.acme]
git = "https://example.com/acme/agent-pack.git"
ref = "v2"

[packs.team]
path = "tools/agent-pack"   # relative to the repo root
Key Type Meaning version integer Format version. 1, the default. exclude array of strings Items not to install, as a path in the pack (skills/brainrc-aws) or after its name (gatework:skills/brainrc-aws); * and ? match. harnesses array of strings Harnesses (from harnesses.toml) that get tool-specific files besides the standard ones. Default: every enabled harness in core's harnesses.toml (never harnesses.local.toml); [] for the standard files only. packs.<key> table One pack. <key> is lowercase letters, digits and -. packs.<key>.enabled boolean Default true. false turns a default pack off. packs.<key>.git string A URL to fetch. Can't start with -. packs.<key>.ref string With git: tag, branch or commit. Default: the remote's default branch. packs.<key>.subdir string With git: the folder of the repo that is the pack, using /. No .., . or leading /. Default: the repo root. packs.<key>.path string A directory inside the repo, relative to the repo root, using /. No .., ~, $ or leading /. packs.<key>.description string A note for people; ignored.
  • Default packs are the tables in core's packs.toml (Gatework). They are on in every project unless brainrc.toml sets enabled = false. A ref alone keeps the default pack's URL; git or path replaces its origin, subdir included.
  • Any other pack needs exactly one of git and path.
  • Unknown keys are errors, so a typo never silently changes what is installed.

docs.title: brainrc.lock
docs.text:
apply writes it; nobody edits it. A second apply with no change to any source leaves it byte-identical.

# brainrc.lock: written by brainrc. Don't edit it by hand.
version = 2
brainrc = "0.7.3"
scope = "project"

[packs.gatework]
git = "https://github.com/brainrc/gatework.git"
ref = "v0.7.1"
commit = "753b9960c5e0d2f1a4b7c8e9d0a1b2c3d4e5f607"

[packs.gatework.files]
"agents/brainrc-analyst.md" = "sha256:3f1c…"
"skills/brainrc-work/SKILL.md" = "sha256:9a0b…"

[packs.team]
path = "tools/agent-pack"

[packs.team.files]
"skills/team-deploy/SKILL.md" = "sha256:5d2e…"

[outputs]
".agents/skills/brainrc-work/SKILL.md" = "sha256:9a0b…"

[blocks]
"AGENTS.md" = "sha256:77c4…"
Key Type Meaning version integer Format version, 2, or 3 when a pack has a subdir. Version 2 adds packs.<key>.permissions and version 3 packs.<key>.subdir; brainrc reads 1 to 3. A lock with no subdir stays at 2, so older brainrc still reads it. A reader refuses a newer version and names the brainrc that wrote it, so brainrc 0.7.7 and older say to upgrade instead of failing on permissions. brainrc string The brainrc version that wrote it, MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. scope string user or project. packs.<key> table Every enabled pack, and nothing for a disabled one. packs.<key>.git string The URL fetched, with any user name or password removed. packs.<key>.ref string The ref asked for (HEAD when the config names none). packs.<key>.subdir string The folder of the repo that is the pack, when the config names one. Its files are listed by their path in that folder. packs.<key>.commit string The commit that ref resolved to: 40 or 64 lowercase hex digits. Git packs only. packs.<key>.path string A path pack's directory as the config wrote it; under the home directory it is written with ~. Path packs have no commit. packs.<key>.files table Every installed file of the pack (below): its path in the pack, using /, to its hash. packs.<key>.permissions table What the pack can do in this scope (permissions): hooks, mcp, tools, domains, each a sorted array of strings, present only when not empty. outputs table Project scope: every file brainrc wrote into the repo, repo-relative, to its hash. blocks table Project scope: files brainrc shares with you (AGENTS.md): the hash of its marked block.

A hash is sha256: and 64 lowercase hex digits, the SHA-256 of the file's bytes. A pack has exactly one of git (with commit) and path. outputs and blocks appear only in a project lock, and only when they have entries; empty files tables are written too.

A pack's installed files are the files brainrc reads from it to install: pack.toml, the file its validator names, rules/*.md (not README.md or *.local.md), each item it installs (every file under skills/<name>/, agents/<name>.md, commands/<name>.md) after the profile and exclude are applied, and, in user scope with hooks installed, every file under overrides/. Symbolic links are followed, so a file is hashed as it is read. __pycache__ directories are skipped.

Determinism. The lock is UTF-8 with \n line endings and ends with one newline. The first line is the comment above. Then come version, brainrc and scope, in that order. Then one [packs.<key>] table per pack sorted by key, its keys in the order git, ref, subdir, commit, or path, each followed by its [packs.<key>.files] table and its [packs.<key>.permissions] table (arrays written one string per line, sorted). Then [outputs] and [blocks]. Every table's entries are sorted by key (by Unicode code point). Keys that aren't bare keys (A-Za-z0-9_-) are written as basic strings. Strings escape ", \ and control characters as TOML basic strings do. The lock holds no timestamps, no host or user names, no credentials and no absolute path to the home directory.

Ready for more. Future keys (pinned commands, more permission records) are added inside packs.<key> or as new top-level tables, with a version bump only for a change an old reader would misread.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
The lock records what each pack can do in its scope, so a pack can't widen it unseen:

Field Entries hooks Each hook its overrides/<harness>/settings.fragment.json adds: <harness> <event> [<matcher>] <command>. User scope, when the profile installs hooks. Also brainrc validator <file> when pack.toml names a validator, in both scopes. mcp Each MCP server in its mcp/servers.toml: name, URL or command and arguments, the variables it reads and its harnesses. User scope, full profile. tools Each installed agent's tools (an agent without them gets (every tool)), each skill's and command's allowed-tools, the fragment's permissions (<harness> allow <rule>, deny, ask), and any other key it sets with its value (<harness> sets statusLine = {...}; a sha256 when over 200 characters). domains Each host the pack's MCP URLs and domain: grants name.

status prints PERMS <pack> + <kind> <entry> for what apply would add and - for what it would remove. apply (and update, and install without --frozen) asks before writing anything when any entry is added or a deny or ask rule is removed, and --yes accepts them. Without a terminal to ask in (CI, a script, a pipe) and without --yes, it refuses and writes nothing; there is no variable that skips the question. Removing any other entry never asks. When update is refused, the git packs it moved go back to the commits the lock pins, since the harnesses link into them.

A machine's first lock has nothing to widen from: its permissions are listed once as PERMS lines and recorded as the baseline. A pack added to an existing lock is a widening. A pack entry in a lock written before permissions were recorded has none; it counts as the baseline only while the pack's files still hash as that lock says, and never for MCP servers and their hosts, since mcp/servers.toml isn't among the hashed files. install --frozen installs only what the lock records, so it never asks and takes no --yes: a widening fails it, and apply is where to review and accept it.

docs.title: Roadmap

The plan lives in GitHub epics: each one groups sub-issues in build order and says how to run them with Gatework (/brainrc-work --campaign gh:<epic>). This page lists every open epic under the release gate it belongs to, matching the GitHub milestones, in the order to start them. Within a gate, the epic's own "Start after" note wins over this order.
