docs.title: JSON Schemas
docs.text:
Each brainrc config file has a JSON Schema that describes it after it is parsed as TOML. brainrc checks the files against them, and an editor that reads #:schema lines (Taplo, Even Better TOML) completes and checks them as you type (packs).

File Schema What it is pack.toml pack.toml.schema.json a pack's manifest (packs) mcp/servers.toml mcp-servers.toml.schema.json a source's MCP servers (formats) harnesses.toml harnesses.toml.schema.json where each tool reads its config (formats) brainrc.toml brainrc.toml.schema.json a repo's project manifest (project) brainrc.lock brainrc.lock.schema.json the user or project lock (project)

To point an editor at the copy for main, put this line at the top of the file:

#:schema https://raw.githubusercontent.com/brainrc/brainrc/main/docs/schemas/pack.toml.schema.json

docs.title: spec-agent (old name)
docs.text: spec-agent is the old name of Gatework's engine. This page moved to Gatework, and the old names are listed in upgrading.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Start here: doctor lists what's wrong with the install on this machine and how to fix each item. It changes nothing.

brainrc doctor

Then find the symptom below. From a clone, run python3 scripts/brainrc.py wherever this page says brainrc.

docs.title: A harness doesn't see a skill, agent, command, or rule
docs.text:
Run brainrc apply. Skills, agents, and commands are symlinks, so edits to existing ones show up at once, but new or removed ones need apply. In copy mode they are copies, so edits need apply too. Rules are different: they're rendered into ~/.config/brainrc/instructions.md, so every change to a rule needs apply, edits included; status lists instructions.md as UPDATE until you do. Start a new session in the tool afterwards.

If you moved a clone or upgraded brainrc, the old links are broken and apply reports each as a CONFLICT. Run brainrc apply --repair from the new location: it relinks every broken link that points at the same item's old location (skills/<name>, agents/<name>.md, ...) and prunes the ones into the old location whose item is gone. status --repair shows the changes first. A broken link to anything else stays a CONFLICT, and your own working links are never touched.

docs.title: Every skill shows up twice, or a hook runs twice
docs.text:
Both the plugin and the brainrc command's links are installed. doctor warns when it sees both in Claude Code or Cursor, and names which to remove. Keep one: in Claude Code, /plugin uninstall brainrc@brainrc (the links also bring the rules and your packs), or set [claude] enabled = false in harnesses.local.toml and run apply. In Cursor, keep the plugin (it brings the rules) and set [cursor] enabled = false, or remove ~/.cursor/plugins/local/brainrc.

If doctor warns that the old plugin ai-config@ai-config is installed, you have the plugin under both names: follow Moving from ai-config.

docs.title: CONFLICT in status or apply
docs.text:
A real file, or a symlink pointing outside brainrc and your packs, sits where brainrc wants a link. brainrc never overwrites it. Look at it, then either:

  • move it into a pack (as a skill, agent, or command) and delete the original, or
  • delete it if you don't need it,

and run apply again. EDITED is a copy apply made in copy mode that has changed since: move the change into its source (or delete the copy), then run apply. CONFLICT on a settings file means it isn't valid JSON: fix it by hand. CONFLICT naming an MCP server means your harness config already defines a server of that name: rename or remove yours (or the registry's), then run apply.

docs.title: Config errors
docs.text:
status, apply, validate, and doctor check harnesses.toml, packs.toml, their .local.toml overrides, and each pack's pack.toml first, and name the file and line:

Message Fix ERROR harnesses.local.toml:3: invalid TOML: Invalid value Fix the TOML on that line (often a missing value or quote). ERROR harnesses.local.toml:2: `claude` must be a table, e.g. [claude] Write [claude] on its own line, then enabled = false under it. ERROR harnesses.local.toml:3: [codex] `enabled` must be true or false Use true or false without quotes. Paths and ref must be quoted strings. WARN harnesses.local.toml:2: unknown key `enabeld` in [claude] A typo: the key is ignored until you fix it. WARN harnesses.local.toml:4: unknown harness [cursr] A typo, or a harness harnesses.toml doesn't list. It still loads.

Errors stop the command before it writes anything; warnings don't.

docs.title: Pack errors
docs.text:
Message Fix pack name `acme` is used by both [work] and [acme] Two packs share one name. Change name in one pack.toml, or set enabled = false for one in packs.local.toml. core is taken. skill `acme-deploy` is defined in both acme and acme2 Rename one. Each pack's items carry its own prefix. When one pack takes over a skill another still ships (such as brainrc/kubernetes beside Gatework 0.8), exclude the other's copy in brainrc.local.toml instead (naming). pack python: no folder `python` in https://github.com/brainrc/packs.git at v0.1.0 That ref has no such folder. Fix subdir or ref in packs.local.toml. The clone stays at the commit it had. pack python: `python` in ... is a link or a file, not a folder subdir must name a folder of the repo, not a link or a file. packs.toml [team]: `subdir` goes with `git` subdir picks a folder of a git repo. For a folder on disk, point path at it. acme:skills/x: pack skills must start with `acme-` Rename the item to start with the pack's prefix. acme:pack.toml: `prefix` must be ASCII lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, ending with '-' Fix prefix in pack.toml, e.g. acme-. acme:pack.toml: `prefix` `aws-` uses the vendor name `aws`, ... reserved for official packs, ... one or two edits from the official name `brainrc` Rename the pack or its prefix to follow the naming rules. acme:pack.toml: requires_core `>=2.0` is not satisfied by core 1.2.3 Upgrade brainrc (upgrading) or the pack, or set enabled = false for it in packs.local.toml. pack acme: no pack.toml at ... Fix the pack's path in packs.local.toml.

validate reports all of these. apply and status check each pack the same way first and write nothing while any of them stands, naming validate --pack <dir> for the pack to fix. See packs.md.

docs.title: Settings backups
docs.text:
Before apply changes a harness's settings file (Claude Code: ~/.claude/settings.json), it copies it next to the original as settings.json.bak-brainrc-<UTC time>. The last 5 are kept, counting old settings.json.bak-aicfg-<UTC time> backups too. No backup is made when the file didn't exist yet. MCP config files (~/.claude.json and the others) are backed up the same way.

The rewritten file and its backup keep the original's permissions, so a 0600 ~/.claude.json stays 0600. If the path is a symlink (a dotfiles-managed settings.json), apply writes through to the link's target and leaves the link in place; the backup goes next to the target.

docs.title: Apply while something else writes
docs.text:
Close Claude Code before apply changes MCP servers: it rewrites ~/.claude.json while it runs.

Message Fix ERROR another brainrc apply is running (lock: <path>) Another apply (or update) holds $BRAINRC_HOME/apply.lock. Let it finish, then re-run. The lock is released when that process exits, even if it crashed, so there is nothing to delete. CHANGED <harness> <file> (changed during apply; close Claude Code and re-run) The file changed after apply read it, so apply left it alone and exited 1. Close the harness that writes it, then re-run.

docs.title: Uninstall
docs.text:
brainrc uninstall --dry-run   # see what goes
brainrc uninstall

uninstall removes every link brainrc made (broken ones too), takes its hooks out of each settings file and the MCP servers it added out of each MCP file, and removes the files and directories that leaves empty. Your own settings, hooks, and servers stay, every file it rewrites is backed up first (*.bak-brainrc-*), and an instructions file init moved aside is put back. It reads which harnesses and source roots apply used from $BRAINRC_HOME/harnesses.json, so it still works after you move or delete the checkout or a pack.

Your local config (harnesses.local.toml, packs.local.toml, rules/*.local.md) and fetched git packs stay in $BRAINRC_HOME; uninstall --purge deletes that directory too, unless it holds files brainrc didn't make (then it says which, and leaves them). Then remove the command: uv tool uninstall brainrc (pipx uninstall brainrc, brew uninstall brainrc), or delete the clone.

docs.title: Every tool call is blocked, or doctor says hook missing
docs.text:
In older installs, a hook whose script had gone (checkout moved or deleted, package removed, Python upgraded) exited 2, which Claude Code treats as a block on every tool call. Run apply to rewrite the hook commands: they now skip a missing script (Cursor's reply "allow"), so the harness keeps working. That also means the guard is off until it's fixed, so doctor checks each one:

Finding Fix <harness>: hook missing: <path> Run apply from the checkout or install you use now; it re-links the hooks dir. <harness>: hook <path> exits <n> on an empty payload Run python3 <path> and read the error (often a Python too old for the guard), then apply. <harness>: hook <path> timed out after <n>s Run it by hand to see where it hangs. <harness>: hook <path> can't run: python3 is not on PATH Install Python 3, or put python3 on the PATH the harness starts with.

docs.title: A guard hook blocked something safe, or missed something risky
docs.text: The Claude Code hooks match command patterns (guardrails.md), so both happen. Open an issue with the exact command or tool call, what the hook did, and what you expected. A fix comes with two tests in tests/test_hooks.py: the risky command, and a safe near-miss that must still pass (for example git push origin x asks, git log doesn't).

docs.title: Your first pack
docs.text:
In this tutorial you build a pack called myteam with one skill for Protocol Buffers, install it into your AI tools, and check that Gatework will load it for .proto files. It takes about 15 minutes. You need Python 3.11+ and git.

A pack is a folder or repo of your own, layered on top of brainrc, so you never edit brainrc itself (packs). This tutorial works from a clone of brainrc so it can run the same commands CI does; with the installed command, type brainrc where it says python3 scripts/brainrc.py, and put packs.local.toml in ~/.config/brainrc/.

Run every command from the brainrc clone unless a step says otherwise. CI runs steps 1-4 of this page on every change (scripts/check_tutorial.py), so they stay accurate.

docs.title: 1. Clone brainrc, install it, and check it
docs.text:
git clone <this-repo> ~/brainrc
cd ~/brainrc
python3 scripts/brainrc.py apply
python3 scripts/brainrc.py validate

apply fetches the default pack, Gatework, and installs brainrc and Gatework into your AI tools. validate should then print a line starting with OK: that counts skills, agents, and commands.

docs.title: 2. Create the pack
docs.text:
new pack writes a pack that validates, then checks it. --yes takes the defaults; without it, in a terminal, it asks for the prefix, the tools you'll edit the pack with, and a ticket system.

python3 scripts/brainrc.py new pack myteam --to ~/src/myteam-ai-pack --yes

You should see OK: with (packs: gatework, myteam) at the end: brainrc, the default pack it fetched in step 1, and yours. The pack's pack.toml sets its prefix, myteam-, which keeps your item names apart from everyone else's, and requires_core, the brainrc versions it works with. The pack also has a facts skill, myteam-facts, a rule that points at it, tripwires, tests and a CI workflow (what each file is for).

docs.title: 3. Add a domain skill
docs.text:
A domain skill, one for a single stack, has four sections: how to validate offline, conventions, a review checklist, and what never to do without approval. The description is what makes an AI tool load it, and the [[extensions.gatework.domains]] row tells Gatework which files load it. new skill --domain writes both, with a line in each section saying what goes there; then fill the sections in.

python3 scripts/brainrc.py new skill protobuf --pack ~/src/myteam-ai-pack --domain '*.proto,buf.yaml' \
  --description "Protocol Buffers schemas for myteam services. Use when changing or reviewing protobuf files."
cat > ~/src/myteam-ai-pack/skills/myteam-protobuf/SKILL.md <<'EOF'
---
name: myteam-protobuf
description: Protocol Buffers schemas for myteam services. Validation, conventions, and a review checklist for *.proto and buf.yaml. Use when changing or reviewing protobuf files.
---

# myteam-protobuf

## Validate (offline)
~~~bash
buf lint
buf breaking --against '.git#branch=main'
~~~

## Conventions
- One package per directory, named after the service and version (`myteam.billing.v1`).
- Never reuse or renumber a field. Reserve removed numbers and names.

## Review checklist
- A field changed type or number: that breaks every existing client.
- New required semantics on an existing message: needs a new version.

## Never without approval
- Publishing generated code or pushing to a schema registry.
EOF
python3 scripts/brainrc.py validate --pack ~/src/myteam-ai-pack

validate should print OK: again. A common mistake is a skill without the prefix. validate then names it, for example myteam:skills/protobuf: pack skills must start with `myteam-`.

docs.title: 4. Enable and install it
docs.text:
Packs are enabled per machine in packs.local.toml, which git ignores. status is a dry run and apply writes.

cat > packs.local.toml <<'EOF'
[myteam]
path = "~/src/myteam-ai-pack"
EOF
python3 scripts/brainrc.py status
python3 scripts/brainrc.py apply
python3 scripts/brainrc.py status | grep 'Everything in sync.'

The first status lists CREATE lines, including ones for myteam-protobuf and myteam-facts in each harness's skills directory. After apply, status prints Everything in sync.

docs.title: 5. Check what your AI tools now see
docs.text:
ls ~/.claude/skills/myteam-protobuf
grep myteam ~/.config/brainrc/extensions.md
python3 scripts/brainrc.py tokens | grep myteam

You should see SKILL.md, a Domains row for `*.proto`, `buf.yaml` naming myteam-protobuf, and the skill's cost in tokens. Gatework reads that Domains row at the start of every ticket, so a ticket touching a .proto file now loads your skill.

docs.title: 6. Put the pack under version control
docs.text:
cd ~/src/myteam-ai-pack
git init -q
git add .
git -c user.name=you -c user.email=you@example.com commit -qm "Add myteam pack"

Push it, and the CI workflow new pack wrote (.github/workflows/validate.yml) checks the pack on every push with the validate-pack action, against the brainrc version it pins (Validate a pack in its own CI). Move that pin, and requires_core, when you test against a newer brainrc.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• examples/pack-acme shows every other pack feature: an intake context skill, a ticket connector, Deliver checks, rules, commands, and tripwires.
  • Packs is the full pack reference.
  • To share the pack with a repo's agents instead of one machine, list it in the repo's brainrc.toml (team setup).
  • To share a domain skill with everyone instead, open a pull request on brainrc/packs: the skill goes in its stack's folder, with an [[extensions.gatework.domains]] row in that folder's pack.toml.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text: Two things move independently: the brainrc command, and the packs it installs.

docs.title: Upgrade brainrc
docs.text:
uv tool upgrade brainrc          # or: pipx upgrade brainrc, brew upgrade brainrc
brainrc apply --repair

Run apply after every upgrade. It refreshes the copy of the guard hooks your tools run, and --repair relinks skills and agents whose links still point at the old version (an upgrade can move the package to a new Python, and Homebrew keeps each version in its own folder).

From a clone, git pull (or git checkout v<X.Y.Z> for a release), then python3 scripts/brainrc.py apply.

What changed in each release is in the CHANGELOG. Changes that affect packs are tagged [pack contract].

docs.title: Move packs to newer versions
docs.text:
apply keeps each git pack at the commit recorded in brainrc.lock, even when its tag or branch moves. To take what the pack's ref points at now:

brainrc update              # every git pack
brainrc update gatework     # or just one

update prints the commits and files that change, then applies and relocks. To move to another tag, change ref in packs.local.toml (or the repo's brainrc.toml) and run apply. An official pack from brainrc/packs moves the same way: change its ref to a newer tag of that repo and keep its subdir.

A new brainrc release can also pin a newer Gatework in its own packs.toml; the next apply fetches it.

docs.title: Gatework 0.9: stack skills moved to packs
docs.text:
Gatework 0.9 no longer ships brainrc-go-service, brainrc-db-migrations, brainrc-terraform, brainrc-aws, brainrc-kubernetes, brainrc-gitops or brainrc-containers. They live, under the same names, in the official packs brainrc/go, brainrc/terraform-aws and brainrc/kubernetes. To keep the ones you use, add their packs to packs.local.toml and run brainrc apply:

[terraform-aws]
git = "https://github.com/brainrc/packs.git"
ref = "v0.1.0"
subdir = "terraform-aws"

An exclude line for one of those skills under gatework: now matches nothing and can go.

docs.title: From ai-config
docs.text:
brainrc's old name, before 0.4.0, was ai-config, with an aicfg command and settings in the old ~/.config/ai-config. If you used the old name:

  1. Remove the old package: uv tool uninstall ai-config (or pipx uninstall ai-config). The aicfg command was removed in 0.5.0: use brainrc.
  2. Move the old settings home: brainrc migrate --dry-run shows the move, brainrc migrate does it and runs apply. With the old AICFG_HOME set, set BRAINRC_HOME to the new place first. Until you migrate, init, status, apply, update, install, uninstall and pin-mcp refuse and write nothing.
  3. Replace the old plugin, as below.

docs.title: Moving from ai-config
docs.text:
The plugin was renamed from the old ai-config to brainrc, and its skills from the old ai-config:<name> to brainrc:<name>. Remove the old one first, or every skill and hook loads twice:

  • Claude Code: /plugin uninstall ai-config@ai-config, then /plugin marketplace remove ai-config.
  • Codex: uninstall ai-config@ai-config and remove its marketplace, per Codex's docs.
  • Cursor: delete the old link ~/.cursor/plugins/local/ai-config.

Then install brainrc@brainrc (plugins). doctor warns until the old plugin is gone.

docs.title: From spec-agent
docs.text:
Gatework's engine was called spec-agent before brainrc 0.7. Its skills and agents now start with brainrc-:

Old name New name spec-agent brainrc-gatework /spec-status, /spec-approve, /spec-resume /brainrc-gatework-status, /brainrc-gatework-approve, /brainrc-gatework-resume ticket-github, ticket-jira, ticket-local brainrc-ticket-github, brainrc-ticket-jira, brainrc-ticket-local kubernetes, unslop and the other domain skills brainrc-kubernetes, brainrc-unslop, ... analyst, verifier and the other agents brainrc-analyst, brainrc-verifier, ... [extensions], [extensions.spec-agent] in pack.toml [extensions.gatework]

Gatework 0.8.0 no longer installs the old names in this table: the next brainrc apply removes their links. A pack that still names one in [extensions.gatework] works with a warning until Gatework 0.9.0. Use the new names. The older /work, /review, /plan, aws and terraform were removed in 0.6.0: use /brainrc-work, /brainrc-review, /brainrc-plan, brainrc-aws and brainrc-terraform.

docs.title: Start a pack for your employer
docs.text: Keep what only your employer's agents should know (internal hosts, ticket keys, review rules) out of brainrc and out of public repositories, in a private pack every colleague turns on.

docs.title: 1. Write it into a private repository
docs.text:
brainrc new pack acme --to ~/src/acme-ai-pack --ticket jira --host acme.atlassian.net --refs 'ACME-*'

--ticket jira adds an [extensions.gatework.ticket] table, so Gatework uses its Jira connector for ACME-* refs. Use --ticket github for GitHub issues, or leave it out. Push the folder to a private repository; its CI workflow checks it on every push (validate in CI).

docs.title: 2. Fill in the facts, not the rules
docs.text: Put hosts, repositories, tools and teams in skills/acme-facts/SKILL.md. It loads only when a task needs it. Keep rules/ for the few things every session must follow, written as a narrower case of brainrc's rules ("in Acme repos, also ..."): rules load into every session on every machine with the pack (rules, context cost).

docs.title: 3. Add what your team checks before a PR
docs.text:
Add a line to deliver_checks for each check Gatework should list at its Deliver gate, and a [[extensions.gatework.domains]] row for each file pattern that should load one of your skills (extensions):

[extensions.gatework]
deliver_checks = ["Deploy plan reviewed by the owning team"]

docs.title: 4. Stop stale facts coming back
docs.text:
When a tool is retired or a host renamed, change the facts skill and add a tripwire for the old name, so validate fails if anyone writes it again (tripwires):

[[tripwire]]
id = "retired-deploy-tool"
pattern = '(?i)\bshipit\b'
message = "shipit was retired. Deploys go through the acme-deploy skill."
allow = '(?i)retired|never'

docs.title: 5. Turn it on
docs.text:
Each colleague adds it by git URL, pinned to a tag, and applies; git uses their own credentials for the private repository (use a pack):

[acme]
git = "git@github.com:acme/acme-ai-pack.git"
ref = "v1.0.0"

To give every agent in one of the employer's repositories the pack, list it in that repository's brainrc.toml instead (team pack).

docs.title: Turn a plugin into a pack
Turn a Claude Code plugin into a pack
docs.text: Move a Claude Code plugin of your own into a pack, so every tool brainrc manages gets its skills, agents, commands and MCP servers, and Claude Code keeps its hooks.

docs.title: 1. Import it
docs.text:
Name the plugin's folder, the one that holds .claude-plugin/plugin.json:

brainrc import ~/src/shipit --name acme --to ~/src/acme-ai-pack --dry-run   # what it would write
brainrc import ~/src/shipit --name acme --to ~/src/acme-ai-pack
In the plugin In the pack skills/<name>/ skills/acme-<name>/, every file in it, with name: changed to match agents/<name>.md agents/acme-<name>.md, with name: changed to match commands/<name>.md commands/acme-<name>.md hooks/hooks.json and the scripts its hooks run overrides/claude/settings.fragment.json and overrides/claude/hooks/ .mcp.json mcp/servers.toml, each server named acme-<name>

Every item name starts with the pack's prefix (naming). A plugin's skills were called /shipit:name; import changes shipit:name, [agent: name] and "name skill" in the items' text to the new names. Each item keeps the rest of its frontmatter and a comment naming the file and lines it came from.

docs.title: 2. Check what it couldn't move
docs.text:
import prints a WARN line for each of these, and leaves them out:

  • A value in a server's env. brainrc writes variable names, never values. An env entry of "${TOKEN}" becomes env_from = ["TOKEN"]; set any other in your environment and add its name to env_from (MCP servers).
  • A server that runs the plugin's own files (${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} in its command): install them somewhere, then add the server to mcp/servers.toml by hand.
  • A hook that runs none of the plugin's files, such as npx prettier --write or a prompt hook: apply knows the pack's hooks by {{hooks_dir}} in their command, so put it in a script in overrides/claude/hooks/ and run that.
  • A link inside a skill: copy what it points at into the skill.

In settings.fragment.json, ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/x became {{hooks_dir}}/x, which apply fills in, and the MCP tool names in hook matchers and agents' tools follow the servers' new names (layout). Test each hook with brainrc.testing in the pack's tests/ (pack tests); examples/pack-homelab has one.

docs.title: 3. Validate, then stop installing the plugin
docs.text:
import checks the pack as validate --pack does. The pack it writes is only the plugin's items: for the rest of what a pack carries (a README, tripwires, tests, CI), start one with brainrc new pack acme and move the imported items into it.

brainrc validate --pack ~/src/acme-ai-pack

Turn the pack on (use a pack), then uninstall the plugin from Claude Code, so its skills and hooks don't load twice.

docs.title: Import the instruction files you have
docs.text:
Move a CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, Cursor, Copilot or Windsurf rules, or a Claude Code plugin, into a pack in one command.

brainrc import PATH ... writes the instruction files you already have as a pack, so they move over in one command. A folder means the files in it that brainrc reads.

Source Becomes CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md one rule per section, in order Cursor: .cursor/rules/**/*.mdc, .cursorrules alwaysApply: true rules and .cursorrules become rules; a rule scoped by globs becomes a skill with a row in Gatework's Domains table for those globs; one with only a description becomes a skill with that description Copilot: .github/copilot-instructions.md, .github/instructions/**/*.instructions.md copilot-instructions.md becomes one rule per section; a path-specific file with applyTo: "**" becomes a rule, one scoped to other globs a skill with a Domains row, one with neither a skill loaded on request, as for Cursor; one for code review only (excludeAgent: coding-agent) is skipped Windsurf: .windsurfrules, global_rules.md, .windsurf/rules/**/*.md .windsurfrules and global_rules.md become one rule per section; a rule file with trigger: always_on becomes a rule, trigger: glob a skill with a Domains row for its globs, model_decision a skill with its description, and manual a skill loaded on request, as for Cursor A Claude Code plugin: a folder with .claude-plugin/plugin.json its skills (every file in each), agents and commands, with the pack's prefix; hooks/hooks.json as overrides/claude/settings.fragment.json, with the scripts its hooks run in overrides/claude/hooks/; .mcp.json as mcp/servers.toml, with variable names in env_from and never a value (from a plugin)

Each file is split at the shallowest heading level it uses more than once (a lone # Title stays with the text under it), and each part becomes rules/NN-<heading>.md with a first-line comment naming the file and lines it came from. Headings inside code blocks don't count. A CLAUDE.md line that is only @path (Claude Code's import) is replaced by that file's rules, and a brainrc project block is left out, since install writes it.

brainrc import ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md --name mine --enable   # write ~/.config/brainrc/imported/mine, load it
brainrc import . --to tools/agent-pack --dry-run          # what a repo's files would become

The pack goes to $BRAINRC_HOME/imported/<name> unless --to names a folder, and is checked as validate --pack would. import never overwrites a folder with files in it; --force replaces an earlier pack there (a folder with a pack.toml), never one that holds a source. --enable adds it to packs.local.toml; for one project, list it in brainrc.toml instead (team setup).

docs.title: Keep your own instructions in a pack
docs.text: Move the instructions you wrote for yourself into a pack, so every AI tool on every machine you use gets them, and brainrc's own files stay untouched.

docs.title: 1. Start from what you have
docs.text:
If you already keep instructions in a CLAUDE.md, an AGENTS.md, Cursor rules or Copilot instructions, import them; each section becomes a rule (import):

brainrc import ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md --name mine --to ~/src/mine --enable

Otherwise, start an empty one and turn it on:

brainrc new pack mine --to ~/src/mine --enable

docs.title: 2. Keep it short
docs.text: Rules load into every session. Put a habit you want everywhere in rules/, and anything longer (how you like a commit message, a checklist) in a skill that loads when it's needed. brainrc tokens shows what each costs (context cost).

docs.title: 3. Carry it to your other machines
docs.text:
Push the folder to a repository (private, if you like), then on each machine:

# packs.local.toml
[mine]
git = "git@github.com:you/mine.git"

brainrc apply

Leave out ref to follow the default branch: brainrc update mine then takes your latest commits (use a pack).

docs.title: Publish a pack for a stack
docs.text: Share what agents should know about one language, framework or platform, for anyone to turn on.

docs.title: 1. Pick a name you can publish
docs.text:
Publish the pack under your GitHub handle, with a prefix that starts with it. Names that look like an official pack's or use a vendor's name are refused (naming):

brainrc new pack jdoe-elixir --id jdoe/elixir --prefix jdoe-elixir-

docs.title: 2. Write one domain skill per stack
docs.text: A domain skill has four sections: how to validate offline, conventions, a review checklist, and what never to do without approval. Its description says when to load it. The tutorial writes one in full.

docs.title: 3. Tell Gatework which files load it
docs.text:
[[extensions.gatework.domains]]
files = "`*.ex`, `*.exs`, `mix.exs`"
skills = ["jdoe-elixir-phoenix"]
reviewer = "brainrc-code-reviewer"   # optional: the agent that reviews these files

docs.title: 4. Say which brainrc versions it works with
docs.text: new pack pins requires_core to the minor series you ran it with, and its CI workflow and pre-commit hook to that release's tag. When you test against a newer brainrc, move all three together (compatibility).

docs.title: 5. Release it
docs.text:
Tag a release, and tell people to pin the tag:

[jdoe-elixir]
git = "https://github.com/jdoe/elixir-pack.git"
ref = "v1.0.0"

A domain skill everyone should get can go into an official pack instead: open a pull request on brainrc/packs that adds the skill to its stack's folder (or a new folder for a new stack) with an [[extensions.gatework.domains]] row in that folder's pack.toml.

docs.title: Share a pack with a team through its repository
docs.text: Give every agent that opens one repository the same rules and skills, on every machine and in CI, whether or not each person has brainrc installed.

docs.title: 1. Write the pack into the repository
docs.text:
From the repository's root:

brainrc new pack team --to tools/agent-pack

It prints the brainrc.toml table that loads it. Delete the pack's .github/workflows/validate.yml and .pre-commit-config.yaml: they only run at a repository's root, and step 4 checks the pack from this repository's CI. A pack your team keeps in its own repository works the same way with git and ref in place of path.

docs.title: 2. List it in brainrc.toml
docs.text:
version = 1

[packs.team]
path = "tools/agent-pack"

docs.title: 3. Apply and commit
docs.text:
brainrc apply
git add brainrc.toml brainrc.lock tools/agent-pack .agents .claude AGENTS.md CLAUDE.md
git commit -m "Add the team's agent pack"

apply writes the pack's skills into the repository (.agents/skills/, .claude/skills/) and its rules into AGENTS.md, and records every file's hash in brainrc.lock (team setup).

docs.title: 4. Check it in CI
docs.text:
Add both checks to the repository's CI: the pack against brainrc, and the agent files against the lock.

- uses: brainrc/brainrc/.github/actions/validate-pack@<brainrc tag>
  with:
    path: tools/agent-pack
- run: pipx run brainrc check

After a change to the pack, run brainrc apply again and commit the new lock with it; check names any file that differs (drift in CI).

docs.title: Use a pack
docs.text: Turn a pack on for this machine, move it to a newer version, or turn the default pack off. For a pack every agent in one repository gets, see team setup.

docs.title: Enable a pack
docs.text:
List it in packs.local.toml (where that file lives), then apply:

[acme]
path = "~/src/acme-ai-pack"   # ~ and $VARS expand; relative paths are relative to this file
# enabled = false             # removes the pack's links and hooks on the next apply

brainrc status   # preview
brainrc apply

Or name it by git URL and let brainrc fetch it, with no clone of your own:

[acme]
git = "git@github.com:acme/acme-ai-pack.git"   # any URL git accepts; private repos use your git credentials
ref = "v1.2.0"                                 # tag, branch, or commit; default: the remote's default branch

apply fetches it into ~/.config/brainrc/packs/acme; after that it works offline. It records the commit the ref resolved to, and a hash of every file it installed, in ~/.config/brainrc/brainrc.lock, and from then on keeps the pack at that commit, even when the tag or branch moves. To move it:

  • brainrc update [<pack> ...] refetches at the ref, prints the commits and files that change, then applies (pinned commits).
  • Changing ref or git fetches the new one on the next apply (status shows a FETCH line).

A repo can hold several packs, one per folder, as brainrc/packs does. Name the folder with subdir:

[python]
git = "https://github.com/brainrc/packs.git"
ref = "v0.1.0"
subdir = "python"

Both refuse a clone with local changes, and stop any git call after 60 seconds. Pin a tag, and bump ref to upgrade. doctor reports a git pack that isn't fetched yet or doesn't match its git and ref.

The lock also records what each pack can do: its hooks, MCP servers, tool grants and network domains. status lists any added (PERMS ... +) or removed, and apply asks before adding any unless you pass --yes (permissions).

docs.title: Turn the default pack off or pin it
docs.text:
A default pack is on unless you turn it off. Gatework is the only one: its engine (the brainrc-gatework skill), its roles, the ticket connectors and the domain skills. It lives in brainrc/gatework, and brainrc's own packs.toml pins it to a release tag, so apply fetches it like any git pack.

In packs.local.toml:

[gatework]
enabled = false        # turn it off: brainrc then installs only its rules and guard hooks

[gatework]
ref = "v<X.Y.Z>"       # pin another Gatework release; its git URL is kept

[gatework]
path = "~/src/gatework"   # work on a clone; replaces the shipped git and ref

brainrc init asks whether to keep it. Gatework 0.8.0 stopped installing its old names (spec-agent, spec-status, kubernetes and the rest); the next apply removes their links (old names).

validate --pack checks a pack against brainrc and the default packs on disk, so a pack that extends Gatework is checked against it once apply has fetched it; until then validate warns. --fetch-defaults fetches them at the versions brainrc pins instead (CI).

docs.title: Validate a pack in its own CI
docs.text:
Check a pack on every push and before each commit, against the brainrc version it pins.

The validate-pack action checks a pack against the core version you pin, and against core's default packs (Gatework) at the versions that core pins, so a pack may use their skills and agents:

- uses: actions/checkout@<sha>
- uses: brainrc/brainrc/.github/actions/validate-pack@<core tag or sha>
  with:
    path: .                  # the pack's directory (default: the repository root)
    # default-packs: "false" checks it against core alone
    # python-version: "3.12" sets one up; by default it uses the python3 on PATH

The ref you pin is the core: GitHub runs the action from that commit of this repository, so there is nothing else to clone. To check before each commit, add the pre-commit hook, which installs brainrc at the rev you pin:

- repo: https://github.com/brainrc/brainrc
  rev: <core tag>
  hooks:
    - id: brainrc-validate-pack
      # args: [pack]          # the pack's directory, when it isn't the repository root

Both run validate --pack <dir> --fetch-defaults, which fetches the default packs at the refs core's packs.toml pins into clones of their own under $BRAINRC_HOME/validate-packs/ (once; later runs reuse them), never the clones apply links.

Without either, clone core at the version you pin and run it yourself:

git clone --depth 1 --branch <core tag> https://github.com/brainrc/brainrc core
python3 core/scripts/brainrc.py validate --pack . --fetch-defaults

What validate --pack checks is listed in the reference.

docs.title: Why packs, and what you trust when you turn one on
docs.text: A pack is the unit brainrc shares instructions in. This page explains why it's a separate unit from brainrc itself, and what keeps a pack you didn't write from doing more than you agreed to.

docs.title: Why a pack, not a fork
docs.text:
brainrc's own rules and hooks are generic: they say how an agent should work anywhere. What an agent needs to know about one employer, team or stack (its hosts, ticket keys, review rules, domain skills) changes on another schedule and often can't be public. Keeping that in a pack means brainrc can be updated without merging into your copy, and a pack can be private, versioned and owned by the people who know its subject.

One pack also reaches every tool. A pack's skills, agents, commands, rules, hooks and MCP servers are written once, and apply renders them into each harness's own format and place. The same pack listed in a repository's brainrc.toml gives every agent that opens the repository the same files, through AGENTS.md and .agents/skills/, whether or not each person runs brainrc.

docs.title: Rules cost every session; skills cost one
docs.text: A rule is loaded into every session on every machine with the pack, so it is paid for whether or not the task needs it. A skill's description is loaded, and its body only when a task calls for it. That is why new pack writes one short rule that points at a facts skill, and why max_always_tokens and brainrc tokens exist: the budget is shared with every other pack and with the work itself (context cost).

docs.title: The trust model
docs.text:
Turning a pack on runs its hooks, starts its MCP servers and puts its text in front of your agents. brainrc can't judge whether that text is good advice, so it makes sure you can see what a pack can do, that it can't change unseen, and that its code runs only where you chose.

  • Names say who it's from. brainrc- and brainrc/ belong to official packs, a published pack's prefix starts with its owner's handle, and names one or two edits from an official name or using a vendor's are refused. Every item starts with its pack's prefix, so one pack can't replace another's skill (naming).
  • What it can do is in the lock. brainrc.lock records each pack's hooks, MCP servers, tool grants and the hosts they reach. apply shows a PERMS line for each new one and asks before writing; in CI, with no one to ask, it refuses. install --frozen installs only what the lock holds (permissions).
  • What it is can't move. The lock pins each git pack to a commit and every file to a hash. brainrc check fails when a file differs, with no network; update is the one command that moves a pack, and it shows what changed first (pinned commits).
  • Its code runs only where you chose. A pack's validator runs inside brainrc only for a default pack, for validate --pack, or when you set run_validator = true for it. Its tests run only from validate --pack on the command line, never from apply or doctor (validator plugins, pack tests).
  • It says which brainrc it fits. requires_core stops apply writing anything when brainrc is outside the range the pack was tested with (compatibility).
  • Old mistakes stay fixed. A pack's tripwires fail validate when a retired tool, host or path comes back in any file (tripwires).

None of this reviews a pack's instructions for you. Read a pack's rules and hooks before you turn it on, the way you'd read a dependency's install script, and pin it to a tag or commit.

docs.title: Packs and Claude Code plugins
docs.text: brainrc also ships as a Claude Code plugin (plugins), but packs need the brainrc command: a plugin could carry a pack's skills, agents and hooks, but not its rules or its Gatework extensions (domains, ticket connector, Deliver checks), which brainrc apply renders, and it reaches only Claude Code. This may change if plugins gain a way to extend another plugin. To move a plugin of your own into a pack, see from a plugin.
